speechtext:
I rise on a short point of order, Mr. Speaker. Basically I want to seek some direction. In this House I think we all appreciate that certain immunities exist regarding the interventions made by members of Parliament in order to ensure that freedom of speech is a reality in this Chamber.
This is the first chance I have had to raise this. I do want to refer once again to something that happened on Thursday of last week regarding some of the comments made by my friend from Portage-Interlake regarding the president of the Public Service Alliance of Canada when he called on two occasions, first suggesting that the president was participating in a despicable act of cowardice and went on to say that he as an individual would rather drown or hang people and so on.
I guess what I am saying is that I really need some ruling or some direction from the Chair. I noticed in reading Hansard of yesterday-unfortunately I was travelling-that an intervention was made by the Chair during Question Period when it was felt that an hon. member from the Liberal Party referred to the comments of a minister as baloney. You felt it was appropriate to intervene at that point and ask the member to retract that statement. He did this. Mr. Speaker, I support this initiative from the Chair.
I saw that one day and on another day a member called someone who is not in this House a coward, despicable and someone who encourages people to drown others and so on. Consequently the person does not have an opportunity to respond to these accusations. It seems to
me that we just cannot let this go on and not have some response by yourself, Mr. Speaker.
When the intervention was first made I asked the member to withdraw the remarks. But in a sense if you looked at his comments he seemed to just add to them. Mr. Speaker, you said that you would review the situation and make the appropriate comment. I appreciate that. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, since I was travelling yesterday and not in the House you were intending to do just that. But I wanted to encourage you particularly in light of the intervention you made yesterday which I thought was appropriate. You said that at the earliest convenience you would give some direction as to how we can maintain the appropriate measure of comment.
We have privileges that encourage free speech. Our comments are not actionable which means we cannot launch a libel suit or defamation suit as a result of comments made here. It is up to us as members of Parliament and particularly, Mr. Speaker, through you to set some sort of measurement of appropriateness. We ask you as the Chair to enforce those measures.
I raise this matter in that most positive way seeking direction from yourself.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make two quick comments on this intervention. The first one is that in principle I very much support what the hon. member is suggesting.
I think the House leader of the New Democratic Party has raised an issue that has been of growing concern to this House. We need to be very careful in our assertions about the reputations of people who are not in this institution and cannot defend themselves. I thought I would want to signal to the Chair my complete support for the Chair being very firm and aggressive when that sort of action takes place. I think we need to do that. I think the Canadian public want us to do that and I am very supportive of the hon. member's assertion on that point.

December 3, 1991
Point of Order
However, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal for a moment with the specific case he raises. I believe this is the statement made by the hon. member for Portage-Interlake at pages 5498 and 5499 of Hansard. I want to read just one paragraph into the record. It is what I think the hon. member is referring to. It says:
Advocating violence against women is unbecoming of all
Canadians. It is a shameful and a despicable act of cowardice.
Intimidation of this nature belongs in the gutter with the filth and the
mire.
My point, Mr. Speaker, is that is an assertion which deals with an advocation of violence against women. I do not think it is an assertion that is aimed at the president of the PSAC although there is the connection made in the statement where the hon. member for Portage-Interlake very much objects to the letter that was sent out by the president of the PSAC. But he does not call the head of the PSAC a coward and he does not accuse him of being despicable. What he says is that if what Mr. Bean has done is advocate violence against women then it is the advocation of violence against women that is shameful and despicable and demonstrates cowardice.
So, Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is a statement directed personally so much at Mr. Bean as it is at the whole issue of violence against women.
I thank the hon. parliamentary secretary. The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my colleague and friend the House leader of the New Democratic Party has raised a very substantive issue concerning the standards that are to be adhered to on the floor of the House of Commons and thereafter the implementation of that particular standard as it applies to the opposition parties and that of the government.
I am happy to hear that the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader subscribes to the principle that my friend and colleague has enunciated here this morning. Yesterday I spoke to you in private about my colleague and where he has used the word "baloney". Then in the midst of Question Period you took it upon yourself to intervene. That ate up some of our time for Question Period by not doing it at the usual time. I would have thought the right time for drawing the attention of the House to the comments that you believed to be
somewhat offensive would have been three o'clock. But at the same time, Mr. Speaker, I seek guidance of the Chair. One has to raise the question how during statements under Standing Order 31 and indeed in other interventions how government members will be policed on the floor of the House of Commons.
We understand, Mr. Speaker, that we are in an opposition party. We understand that certain rules and Standing Orders do indeed apply to us. But we would hope that in the future they would apply to all members of the House. I seek the guidance of the Chair as to how it intends to police some of these aspects. On first appearances, Mr. Speaker, some members have contemplated out loud that maybe the standard that we are all hopefully trying to live by is not in some circumstances being implemented fairly or accordingly to all members of Parliament.
The parliamentary secretary is shaking his head. If he wishes to participate in debate then he should participate in the debate. He should not use body language to try to intimidate those of us who are trying to seek guidance from the Chair on a very important matter. If the parliamentary secretary does not believe that what we are raising is sufficiently important enough let him say so. We seek the guidance of the Chair concerning the standards that the Chair is trying to utilize on the floor of the House of Commons for all members, not just opposition members.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same point of order. My concern is that I think the House leader of the Liberal Party is very close to an assertion against the Chair. I am sure he did not intend it.
I think it is very clear that all members of the House would support the Chair in coming down on members for inappropriate behaviour no matter which side of the aisle they sit on.
I want to say very clearly, Mr. Speaker, that I am sure that is not what the hon. member intended in his remarks. I am sure what he said is that he wanted to see it applied fairly. All of us would certainly support that.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a very short comment and refer to the fact that the points raised by my hon. friend are technically correct.
December 3, 1991

I think being fair is something that we would like to always work toward as an appropriate goal. If people had read carefully what the president of PS AC was doing we would know full well that he was not personally advocating violence against women.
I do not know who determines the government's speaking list but I notice that this issue was raised three times on that day. There were two statements during Question Period where they incorrectly referred to Mr. Bean as being vice-president of the New Democratic Party. Of course he is not.
To take a letter and probably unconsciously and certainly inadvertently distort its intent is incorrect. It is not that this never happens but when we raise issues about one of us in this House it is done knowing full well that that individual will have an opportunity to stand up and defend himself or herself.
I think it is an unfortunate initiative to attack someone in such a vicious way who is outside this House. This is with the knowledge that as long as those comments are made here they are not actionable and if they were made outside the door you would probably end up in a court of law.
I suspect we all share this. I appreciate the comments made by my colleague the parliamentary secretary to the government House leader who says that he even now supports the general thrust of the argument.
It is for that reason that I think we would like to call on you to give us some guidance as to the appropriate way to proceed in the future.

I appreciate very much the tone of the intervention of the hon. member for Kamloops. I appreciate the other interventions that have been made today.
This matter arose several days ago. To be very frank with the House I am still looking at it.
There is an issue here which is not quite as easy to resolve as might at first seem. First, a particular incident took place outside the Chamber. The Chair is not in any particular position to know what exactly took place outside the Chamber except what I may have heard.
Second, moving away completely from the incident to which we have been referring, we have matters that get
Point of Order
into the public domain outside the Chamber. It is sometimes difficult to find the line between what is inappropriate to mention or comment with respect to them and what is appropriate.
I think that the point that was made in general terms that we ought to constrain ourselves considerably in making comments about someone outside this Chamber which would in fact be defamatory under the laws of our country if made outside the Chamber is something which we should consider.
I will try to find a way of expressing this which will give us some guidance. I have been concerned that the use of highly suggestive language or innuendo sometimes on both sides of the House with respect to people or their associations with people can be very demeaning indeed.
This certainly moves the House to a response of irritation or anger which of course leads us to disorder.
I accept the interventions of hon. members that this is a matter which does require some careful thought. I will try to respond in a way that is helpful.
I hope that yesterday's incident is not taken as any indication that there is one standard for one side of the House and another standard for the other, or even one standard for those members who are close enough to the Chair that I can hear when they say something that is not appropriate, as opposed to those members at the very far end of the Chamber. Quite frankly, I cannot hear these comments most of the time.
I think the hon. member who was corrected by me and withdrew and apologized, was hurling words directly at a minister while the minister was responding. I felt that under the circumstances it was appropriate to stop it.
I just want to make it very clear that if I hear comments thrown by government members at hon. members opposite who are putting questions in the same manner, as long as I can hear them, I will certainly rule them out as far as being proper. I want to assure you the Chair is trying to make sure the law falls equally on both sides of the Chamber.
I am frankly heartened by members' comments this morning on this matter, and I think that it indicates a general sense in the Chamber that we do have to make an extra effort to make sure that the decorum of this

December 3, 1991
Privilege
place is acceptable, not just to each other, but also to the public.
In this regard I want to make it very clear that one can either extol or deplore television, but it is here. One thing it has done is give a lot of Canadians a chance to see what we do in the Chamber. While this may have helped some of them see what we are doing in terms of policy and substance, it has also given a lot of people a chance to see things that we do that they do not appreciate. I think that we are bound to take that into account. Certainly this morning's discussion is helpful to me and I hope that I will be able to respond in a way that is helpful to the Chamber.

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday I gave notice in regard to what I believe is a point of privilege.
It is probably the most important statement that I have made in my nine years as a parliamentary member for the riding of Timiskaming. I refer to Hansard, page 5508, of November 28 and the comments made by the member from Sudbury.
The question is in regard to my honesty and integrity. I want to stand before the House today as someone who has represented a riding and has been here for three elections.
The allegations have caused damage to myself, my family and the riding of Timiskaming which I have represented for nine years.
I would like to take a moment to review and set the record straight. I believe that when accusations and allegations are made in this House and transmitted back to your ridings, it is very difficult to be able to stand up and defend them, putting matters straight once and for all.
A year ago, tenders were called for a building in Kirkland Lake. The first round of tenders were all too high. The second round of tenders, numbered project 2000 were disqualified. The second tender was from a company named Cohole construction of Kirkland Lake.
I just want to read a couple of paragraphs in a letter that was sent to Mr. Young Hong, President of Cohole Development Corporation on November 27, 1991.
I wish to re-confirm the advice given you by my staff October 16, 1991 and reiterated in my November 15, 1991 letter to you that Public Works Canada has terminated its contract with Cohole Development Corporation to provide the necessary space. It should be clearly understood that our decision to terminate the contract is based on two factors.
First, as a result of a loss of financing for this project by Cohole Development, your contractor stopped work in September, 1991 thereby placing the project at serious risk. You were unable to secure alternative financing, even after several extensions granted by us to October 16, 1991 and therefore we terminated the contract as we had no guarantee that Cohole Development would be able to complete the project.
You may also recall that at a meeting in your office February 21, 1991, officers of this department and a DVA official discussed the requirements of the project with you and you were advised at that time that a $2 million bond would be required as part of the contract.
The purpose of the bond is to protect the Crown in the event you were unable to complete the project, thereby minimizing our risk by providing funds to offset the costs of leasing interim space.
You may also recall that officials on my staff advised you again on June 21, 1991, at the time the contract was awarded to you, of the requirement for a $2 million bond.
Public Works then went to the third tender, a company called Anthony Kemp Architects Inc. A reference on page 5508 of Hansard, states my brother-in-law was called in as being part of the ownership of this.
I place before you today a letter from Anthony Kemp which states that "as a point of information the sole shareholder of 926260 Ontario Limited is Anthony Kemp. Should this company be successful in this endeavour, the ownership of the said company will be widened to include the following individuals: Anthony Kemp, Garry Fairhurst, Warren Beamish, Norman Seymour, Robert Chafee and Peter Balan. Mr. Gary Watkins does not have and will not have any pecuniary or other interests in 926260 Ontario Limited."
December 3, 1991

Privilege
I also lay before you the different bids: Project No. 926260 of $9,630,000 and Cohole Construction of $9,570,000.
It was also accused that my brother-in-law is a shareholder in the land. I would like to quote from a letter from chartered accountants, Cook Hawley Marks:
We have reviewed the shareholder records as presented in the
attached chart, and confirm that Mr. Gary Watkins, through 510177
Ontario Limited and the First Watkins Family Trust, have a minority
interest of 28.69% in Nelson Bros. Construction Limited.
This is the property I have been accused of having an interest in.
I would like to end by saying that the value of the property in question at DVA bid was $500,000. In addition, we would have paid relocation costs for the Nelson Bros, operation which would be deducted from the $500,000.
In December 1988, long before DVA, we had an appraisal done on the property. It was valued at $558,600. We also have the option on the value of the land at $810,000. On that basis it can be concluded that Gary Watkins is not getting any type of benefit from our involvement in the DVA project.
I feel very sorry for the individuals who were involved with Cohole construction. That development was strictly between Cohole and Public Works. The unfortunate part about it is individuals started to do work believing that Cohole had the financing in place.
If you have been in business for 18 years, you check to see whether your creditors have the funds or not. This was not done. I must say, Mr. Speaker, it has been a very difficult time for me and my family to hear allegations like this made against me, my family and the people that I have represented for nine years.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, in fairness, allegations have been made in this House, and we should once and for all be able to clear such allegations and not allow them to happen.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first thing I want to say is that the hon. member said yesterday, I gather, that I had made allegations with regard to him or his involvement in the termination of the contract for the DVA building in Kirkland Lake.
This inference is totally unwarrant. I asked a question of the Minister of Public Works and I will quote it:
"I want to know the real reason behind this nonsense", and it is in Hansard, as you saw, "is it because the owner of the second site and the member for Timiskaming just happen to be brothers-in-law?" It is a true statement. The owner of the site being considered is Nelson Brothers Construction. The hon. member for Timiskam-ing's brother-in-law happens to be a shareholder and the vice-president of that company. I do not for one minute infer any wrongdoings on the part of the hon. member, absolutely none. On the other hand, the brother-in-law is involved. I will tell you that no one believes that one can be responsible or be one's brother-in-law's keeper, especially not me. I have eight brothers-in-law and I will tell you right away that I do not pretend to have any say in what they do with their lives.
The whole question of this contract has very different sides to it. I will tell you the version that I have been told. Yes, there was one tender and it was turned down. I was told that it was turned down because the zoning was not in place when the people put in their bids. There was a second tender and on June 21, Cohole Development received a letter saying: "We have accepted your tender. Please proceed to construct the site."
On July 16 construction began. On July 18 there was a sod-tuming ceremony. Let me remind the hon. members that there was no mention and no amount of a callable bond in the contract. The amount was just specified as an amount deemed to be reasonable in some way, shape or form and that is fine. Construction began on July 16 and continued until some time after September 23 at which time Cohole Development received a letter stating that Public Works Canada wanted a $2 million callable bond.
Now if you come from northern Ontario, you know how difficult it is to deal with bankers. I will tell you that yes, Cohole Development had some difficulty in obtaining the $2 million bond. There was no extension granted and no letters sent. There was a meeting held in October in Toronto at which time another alternative was put forward. The gentleman involved waited for an answer from Public Works and received no answer until November 15 when he was advised that the contract was terminated, period.
Since then, Cohole Development has come up with the $2 million bond. I have made repeated attempts to question the Minister of Public Works to make sure that he treated this whole thing as fairly as possible, because

December 3, 1991
Routine Proceedings
there is a great deal of money invested in that site. A lot of the construction work has been done. There are contractors in all areas of northern municipalities who stand to lose a great deal of money. That is how I became involved in this question, because some of the contractors are in my riding and they contacted me. They said: "What is happening? Why are we being treated this way?"
The government keeps saying that it is going to this new contractor. The tender from the new contractor is no longer active so they have to get new prices from him. The story goes on.
Meanwhile, I am told today that the owner of Cohole Development is delivering a $2 million callable bond to the people in Toronto. I am asking that they continue to look at this matter, to stop the massive losses, not only of those contractors but of the government itself. It has invested many dollars in this project.
When the foundations are in, the site has been cleared, the steel has been done and the architectural work has been done, it is a serious business to suddenly change the site completely. They are going from one end of town to a completely new site owned by Nelson Brothers Construction, there is no doubt in my mind.
I will tell you that I hope the hon. member for Timiskaming will lead the way in making sure that the government treats absolutely everyone as fairly as possible.

I will hear the hon. member for Timiskaming in a moment, but I may be able to assist the House.
I have listened very carefully to both sides because the issue is complicated, but the issue that I have to resolve is simply this: in the way the question was put, is the hon. member for Sudbury out of order or has there been a breach of privilege with respect to the position of the hon. member for Timiskaming.
I remind hon. members who may want to say something about this that this is the quote: "I want to know the real reason behind this nonsense. Is it because the owner of the second sight and the member for Timiskaming just happen to be brothers-in-law?"
That was then denied by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works. Someone then shouted out: "It sure helped the brother-in-law", and another hon. member said: "all in the family".
I have to take the mood that was created by the question somewhat into account. That is basically where the Speaker has to decide whether those words were appropriate under the circumstances, whether they were something that was a breach of order in the House or whether they go further.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, your words are exactly all that I want to be concerned about.
It is strictly a business agreement between Public Works and the tenderers. My concern is to clear my name and my family name.

I think in keeping with the other matter which we discussed a little earlier this morning, I am going to look at this carefully and consider it.
I do point out that however I decide, I think hon. members can see how when an imputation is made by way of a question or by a response by a minister, it becomes very personal and can be hurtful. There is difficulty that it creates in the Chamber and with each other.
I am going to look at it and see if I can come down with a procedural response which is appropriate. I thank the hon. member for Sudbury. I know she had some difficulty being here yesterday. I received that message very early in the morning and I appreciate the fact. I hope that the hon. member would pass on to her staff our appreciation. That message was brought.
I appreciate the tone set by the hon. member for Timiskaming in bringing what certainly is to him a painful matter to the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to present a petition signed by numerous residents of the province of Ontario and various small communities, most of them farming communities.
These petitioners are concerned that the government is about to trade away the opportunity for them to operate marketing boards under the GATT round of negotiations which are currently under way.
The petitioners call upon the government to hold the Canadian system up as an example to all the world, to stiffen its resolve and ensure that article XI and the rights that accrue to Canada thereunder are not traded away by this government which seems bent on such an idea.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present seven petitions, containing approximately 300 signatures.
The citizens are from Burlington, Stoney Creek, Hamilton, Beamsville, Brantford, Ancaster, Kitchener, Grimsby, St. Catharines, Caledonia, Hannon, Dunnville and Binbrook. These citizens are petitioning the Government of Canada in support of the parents of Nina DeVilliers who was murdered on August 9, 1991. The petitioners call upon Parliament to recognize that crimes of violence against persons are serious and abhorrent to society and ask that the Criminal Code of Canada, the Bail Reform Act and the Parole Act be amended accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure of presenting three petitions today. The first I would have liked to have been able to present yesterday, but it was not possible to do so. It is in respect of constituents of mine of Ukrainian heritage who have asked the federal government to recognize the
Routine Proceedings
independence of Ukraine, subject of course to the referendum indicating that desire for independence.
I rejoice with them as do many, many Canadians throughout the land with respect to the referendum and the recognition that the government has given to Ukraine.

The second petition is in respect of the goods and services tax on reading materials; magazines, books and newspapers.
The petitioners point out that there has been no such tax since the beginning of Confederation. They also indicate that it is counterproductive, it goes against the whole notion of a democratic society that is supposed to be well informed and a society, of course, that strives for excellence through education. Of course, these vehicles are important ones to the development of our citizenry.

My final petition is in respect of education. It is a criticism of a government that talks about competitiveness, productivity, establishing a learning culture, when it has indeed this year cut a half billion dollars in transfer payments to the provinces, as well as placing a 3 per cent administrative fee on student loans.
The petitioners ask that the government rescind these regressive measures so that we can send our young people to college and university in order that they can find the jobs that will contribute fully to Canada.
100TH ANNIVERSARY OF UKRAINIAN CANADIANS

I rise to present a couple of petitions you would be interested in, Mr. Speaker, being that it is the 100th anniversary of the Ukrainian Canadians coming to our country.
These petitions come from the towns of Canora, Rama and the city of Yorkton. They present a petition that I wanted to table yesterday but it is still just as relevant today.
The undersigned petitioners call upon Parliament to urge the Government of Canada to give genuine support to the people of Ukraine by officially recognizing Ukraine's independence in establishing full diplomatic relations with the people of Ukraine immediately following their referendum, which took place on Tuesday.

December 3, 1991
Routine Proceedings
As I said, Mr. Speaker, it has been signed by many people, like Metri Dutchak in Canora, and you can go through the list and find people like Olga Rusnak in Yorkton and many, many others who have made a great contribution to this country who were celebrating the referendum results on Sunday along with a lot of others of us.

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me this morning to present a petition on behalf of a number of citizens from Kamloops, British Columbia, who are concerned about the ability of the RCMP to fulfil its mandate.
In conversations they have commented on the increasing numbers of break and enters, minor petty crimes, and so on, just as a result of what they perceive to be the inability of the RCMP to do its job. They are calling upon the Government of Canada to ensure that proper funding for the RCMP exists to enable it to fulfil its mandate.

On another issue, Mr. Speaker, a very important issue, the petitioners are from a variety of communities in British Columbia. They have heard the news that a Vancouver-based firm with contacts in California has announced its intention to proceed with a plan to dam the North Thompson River at Valemount, British Columbia, in an effort to divert water into the San Diego, California area.
Mr. Speaker, you will recall that this is part of the North American Water and Power Alliance Plan to divert Canadian rivers into the United States, either in whole or in part, and they call upon the Government of Canada to announce categorically that Canadian river water is not for sale.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say from the outset that this is probably my longest speech since I started last evening at about 5.45 and here I am a day later still going. I can assure my constituents that I did not speak throughout the entire night. I am not that long-winded.
I must say, as I mentioned last evening, that this is a very complex and technical bill. I want to continue where I left off when I was speaking last evening about transportation in my riding as it applies to the bill and as it may be affected. I mentioned the Charlo airport in my riding and how important it is to the riding and how we have lost the weather station at that airport, although another weather station was located at another airport. I want to say from the outset that I am not against improvements in other areas, other communities, but I do not believe we should rob Peter to pay Paul. I believe when there is a new item to be taken and new programs coming out, everyone should have an equal opportunity,
Government Orders
but where there are existing facilities in place they should remain and not move at the expense of that community.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to adopt certain measures to implement the budget tabled on February 26 this year, measures that clearly reflect part of the government's strategy for reducing the deficit. However, if we are to understand the strategy as a whole, we should also consider the approaches to controlling inflation that were agreed on with the Governor of the Bank of Canada. Briefly, the measures contained in this bill are being taken at a time when we are experiencing the first made-in-Canada recession, a recession deliberately brought about to control inflation.
During the pre-recession period, we had very high interest rates which had a very negative impact on the federal government's deficit. The cost of servicing the debt, already very high, increased by 28 per cent over two years, before the present budget.
But consider what happens during the recession. During the recession, unemployment and unemployment insurance payments go up. There is also an increase in welfare payments, which during the last recession in 1981-82 went up by 32 per cent. We all know that health care costs, which normally increase by 2 or 3 per cent plus inflation, because of our aging population increase even faster during a recession. And we know that post-secondary education costs also increase faster during a recession, because students tend to stay in college and university.
During the recession, we also see a drop in inflation and interest rates. So what is the impact of all these measures on budgets? Apparently, the federal government is transferring all the costs of the recession to employees and employers by incredibly increasing unemployment insurance contributions by 24.5 per cent in the last budget and another 7 per cent not long ago. The remaining costs of the recession are being transferred to the provinces.
The measures before the House today contain all the tools the federal government needs to avoid recession-induced costs in the areas of health care, social assistance and post-secondary education. The provinces will have to shoulder all these costs, which are, and will be, very substantial.
At the same time, interest rates are going down-for instance, the government predicted that interest rates would be around 9 per cent, while they are now down to 7 per cent-and as a result, the federal deficit will become more manageable. Of course, the government kept the benefits of declining rates and transferred to businesses, individuals and the provinces the costs of rising rates in a recession.
If that keeps up, in a few more weeks, the federal government will brag that it can control its deficit, when in fact it passed it on to the provinces and businesses.
Yesterday I heard the Prime Minister say that he was reluctant to call an economic conference, as requested by the provinces, and I understand that very well. He even dared to say that would force the provinces to control their budgets. What will the provinces do to control their budgets? They will raise taxes or do what Quebec did: pass the costs on to the municipalities. Transferring costs to the municipalities will also result in tax increases. Higher university tuition fees have become the main cause of inflation.
We are at a point where we are in danger of not reaching our inflation objectives, precisely because the federal government is passing costs on to the provinces, municipalities and universities.
For the first time, in this morning's Globe & Mail, a group of 17 economists consulted in forecasting institutions told us that Canada's economic growth is likely to be less than predicted, that Canada's current account deficit will increase considerably and that inflation will be higher.
I thought that was impossible after such drastic measures had been taken. Inflation is likely to be higher because the only way that local and provincial governments can get out of the situation in which the federal government has put them is to raise taxes considerably and thus add to inflation.
Therefore, I think that some balance must quickly be restored. You know that in the 1980s, the federal government spent like mad and ran up huge deficits. For a while, I think we were right to believe that the deficit had gone out of control. Of course, our debt is unacceptably high. We must reduce the deficit; we must also try to keep lower inflation rates. But with such drastic measures as we have taken, we risk not only keeping the economy in a deep recession but also fuelling inflation.
December 3, 1991

A change of course is in order. For an example of the federal government's past spending habits, refer to the latest report of the Economic Council of Canada. Of course, the federal government's fiscal capacity is mortgaged for several more years, until 1994-95, but we are told that after 1995-96, there may be some room to manoeuvre. Room to do what? It is purely theoretical, because the expenses that are harder to control have been transferred to the provinces and we realize increasingly that they will be unable to assume them fully.
For the first time Ontario's deficit will reach $10 billion. The Minister of Finance of course was prompt to blame the Ontario govemement for everything. It is a fact that it did increase its spending by $800 million, but had they not injected these new funds in an effort to boost the economy, Ontario's deficit would still have been close to $9 billion and would have gone on forever.
With the new distribution put in place as a result of Bill C-20, we can be sure that the provinces, all of them, will have increasing deficits and I would not be surprised that, within a few months, they saw their credit rating drop drastically in terms of their borrowing capacity.
As we know, in general the cost of borrowing is higher for the provinces than for the federal government. Analysts in growing numbers anticipate that the gap will widen even further. So, by transferring its deficit over to the provinces, of course the federal government pressures provinces and municipalities to cut their spending. By so doing, it is also creating inflation and as a result the cost of financing such deficits will skyrocket. The rate of borrowing for provinces and municipalities is always at least 75 percentage points higher than for the federal government and is likely to go up another full point or even to 1.25 points in the next few months, which means additional costs for no reason.
And that is not all. Let us keep in mind that, even if we could find a way out of this one and if somehow the federal government still had room to manoeuvre, there is no guarantee that these spending choices would suit the Canadian people. Let me give you some figures. We are told that provinces are still receiving payments and that is true, to a point, but the amounts are cut drastically and much more so than federal spending is curtailed.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-20 which I think is a significant piece of legislation not only in terms of fiscal management but in terms of social policy in Canada.
I had an interesting experience in the last couple of weeks, talking with a number of young people in my riding, people who are the same age as my son and daughter, in their mid-twenties. We got to talking about the present threat to our national health care program. Much to my surprise I found out that people in that age
Government Orders
group simply took our national health care system for granted.
They assumed that when you went to the hospital you would not have to pay, that you would receive a high level of care and that you would not be required on admittance to prove that you were financially able to afford the care. They took for granted that if you needed to go to a doctor you simply went to a doctor, you did not first of all consider your financial position and determine whether you were financially able to go to seek medical care.
I think it is important when we start talking about this bill that we remember very clearly that that has not always been the case in Canada.
I remember very clearly while growing up that I had an older brother who developed a major illness. At that time we were living in a small prairie town in southern Alberta very near the American border. He spent periods of time in hospital in Lethbridge.
The financial resources of my family were strained to the point that they could no longer afford to provide him with the necessary medical care. It was finally arranged that this youngster who was then in his early teens would have to go to seek medical care at a mission hospital north of Edmonton, hundreds of miles away from his home and his family, simply because the mission hospital was funded by the United Church and was prepared to give the necessary medical treatment without immediate payment by my parents. Canadians of my children's age simply do not believe that. They find it totally incomprehensible that that kind of thing could have taken place in Canada.
I had another experience just before I was elected to this House when I was travelling in New Zealand. My mother who is getting on in years joined us for a period of time. She fell and broke her ankle. We thought nothing of immediately seeking out the best medical care available. Much to our surprise we found out that in New Zealand through an accident insurance scheme much like our Workers' Compensation Board the medical expenses of all accident victims were paid for. This includes even foreign residents.
We got to know a number of other people in the hospital. One of them was a woman from the United States who also had the misfortune of falling and breaking her leg which was compounded in a number of places and had difficult breaks. It resulted in her being in

December 3, 1991
Government Orders
hospital in New Zealand for a number of months before she could be transported back to the United States.
I ended up driving her back to the airport and she told me that she and her husband had just retired. He had to go back to the United States because he could not stay in New Zealand. They were not wealthy but they were comfortable and had been planning an active life in retirement. She said that if she had fallen in the United States they would have been financially ruined even with the fact that they had some medical coverage. They would have been absolutely financially decimated to the point that they probably would have had to file for bankruptcy. Certainly they would not have been looking forward to their retirement years with any assets or comforts.
I think Canadians should start remembering that by taking our health care system for granted we are in danger of losing it. This legislation is part of a consistent process of erosion of our national health care system.
Our health care system did not come about easily in this country. It was gained through foresight and struggle after having been introduced by Tommy Douglas in Saskatchewan. It is important to remember that is where the initial and decisive fight for the establishment of medicare took place. The people who were opposed to it were very powerful people. They were the Liberal opposition and doctors. Other special interest groups staged a strike and fought desperately to try to preserve their rights and their privileges and prevent a universal health insurance system.
That battle was won and finally the federal government was forced into bringing in national medicare on a federal level.
This program has been successful in ensuring that all Canadians have access to a high standard of health care.
We have now had a series of attacks on this by the present Tory government. I will not go into the history of the initial 50:50 program and how that program was eroded when the block funding came in. It is important for this House and the Canadian public to understand that the present Established Programs Financing which
was put in place in the late 1970s was based on the federal government transferring to the provinces money for post-secondary education and health care. It was not based on the amount of money spent by the provinces but on the growth in population and the growth in GNP.
The federal government tried to make much of the fact that the health care costs of the provinces have gone up dramatically and they have. The federal government has tried to make much of the fact that the provinces have to contain the cost of health care and they do. The formula that has existed for transferring of moneys had nothing to do with those things. It had only to do with the increase in the GNP. If there was no increase in the GNP the federal government did not increase its contribution to the provinces other than for the increase in the population.
This government has decided to unilaterally change that formula. Being from British Columbia I figure that the government must have somehow taken lessons from the previous Socred administration in that province. Maybe it was when the hon. Minister of Justice switched from being a Socred provincially and became a Tory federally. She came down from British Columbia to Ottawa and brought the Socred way of handling their fiscal incompetence. Now it is called offloading.
The government does not bother to control its own expenditures on advertising. It does not even bother to try to control its own expenditures on the growth of government or in areas where it has direct responsibility. It simply offloaded the problems on to municipalities, school boards and hospitals by cutting their funding.
It simply said: "We know we cannot fiscally control our expenditures but what we can do is simply freeze the moneys we will transfer to other levels".
This is what the government has now adopted. The Socred approach to fiscal management is simply: "Let us offload our deficit and debt on somebody else. Let us offload on the provinces. We will simply decide that we are not going to continue with the formula for transferring of payments. We will cut back". When it got away with cutting back to 2 per cent or 3 per cent less GNP it decided to zero it. This bill now extends that zeroing for five years. It simply says: "Let us wash our hands of any
December 3, 1991

responsibility and offload all of those problems on to the provinces".
What does that mean in terms of our national health care? It means a number of things. First and foremost it means that the provincial governments have dramatically less money to spend on national health care. The cumulative effect of these cuts on health care have been estimated as being $62.4 billion. I am not talking about post-secondary education. In the final years it will amount to around $10 billion a year in lost revenue. I make it clear again that this is lost revenue based on the increase in GNP. It is not based on costs or anything else. This is money that the provincial governments had anticipated. They thought they were in a fiscal arrangement they could count on to build their health care systems around.
It has been devastating already. Some of the weaker provinces, particularly the Atlantic provinces, have had to make dramatic cutbacks to their health care system. Newfoundland in one fell swoop had to lay off 10 per cent of its nursing staff. That is just year one. Wait till the cumulative effects of year three, four and five take place. Even wealthy provinces are feeling the economic pinch. British Columbia will have lost over $5 billion by the year 2000. This year alone it is losing about $500 million.
This has tremendous impact on local communities' ability to deliver health care. What happens is the province is then forced to offload their loss of revenue on to local communities and local hospitals.
My community of Surrey North is one of the fastest growing communities in Canada. We simply have been unable to get the funds to keep up with the necessary health care services that are needed. We only have 1.1 acute hospital beds per 1,000 population. The provincial average is 3.3. In Surrey 40 per cent of the people have to leave to get basic health care. We are 34 public health nurses short. We are 27 health inspectors short of meeting the needs of that community. I think it is important to note that those last two figures are probably more critical than the loss of acute care beds. We all know that one of the things we have to do is change our health care system from a treatment of chronic or acute illness to a health prevention system. But it is often those soft health prevention programs that suffer when there are arbitrary and unnecessary cuts in payments.

There is another thing that is happening concerning the loss of transfer payments and that is the federal government's ability to maintain a national health care system with national standards. The federal government will no longer be transferring cash to Ontario and Quebec by 1995, 1996 and 1997 because of the cutbacks under this bill. It does that in two ways, through two entirely different programs. The first is the Established Programs Financing, which gives all provinces the same per capita amount. Then there is the other program, called equalization, whereby the less well-off provinces receive supplementary sums of money from the federal government. These are the two main transfers of funds from the federal government to the provinces.

In 1991-92, it will be $20.4 billion and in 1992-93, $20.6 billion, under the Established Programs Financing or EPF only. As I said, this is paid equally throughout Canada on a per capita basis.

They have taken apart those things that have brought Canadians together. They have turned it into a country that has region against region. Why? Because there is nothing left held in common.
We sell off this Crown corporation. We destroy the post office. We rip apart medicare. There is not much of a nation left. After eight years of Tory rule they are destroying this country and Bill C-20 is the prime example of it. Exhibit A, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Remember the deficit.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Here we go about the deficit again.
Their problem is that they do not listen very well. I say, let us deal with the deficit, but let us ask the President of the Treasury Board to deal with the problem identified by his own research and by his own government agency. It is: You had better recapture some revenue and you better get your interest rates down, because it has nothing to do with social spending.
I know they have trouble reading. I know the former minister of trade and industry, Mr. Crosbie, never read the free trade act. That is why we got into that horrible mess. Now we have the President of the Treasury Board saying that he does not read his own economic analysis from his own agency called Statistics Canada, which described for him what the problem in the deficit was.
I suggest, in all charity and kindness, that the best solution for Canada in the few months remaining for this government would be to give its members a remedial
Government Orders
reading course so they can begin to read their own documents and understand what is going on here.
Most of all, it might enable them to read Bill C-20. It sets out in black and white that beginning in the middle part of this decade and ending in the year 2003, the federal government will no longer be directly involved in the support of health care and higher education.
As a result, our ability to maintain the five principles of accessibility, portability, comprehensibility and public administration will disappear because we will no longer have any leverage to exercise on the provinces.
If a province wants to introduce user fees, it can introduce user fees. In fact, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, my co-parliamentarian from Manitoba, the member for Provencher says maybe we should have user fees. His other colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, at the health meeting in Winnipeg in September agreed. He is prepared to accept asymmetrical programming in health care. That is, if some province wants user fees and another one does not, he will buy that. He does not care about that.
I would submit to you that as soon as we begin to surrender on that front, as soon as we begin to say that there will be a health care system graduated for your ability to pay and those with the most money get the best care, that will be really the end of this country as we have known it.
It will be the end not just in terms of health care itself in what we provide, not just in terms of money, but also in terms of values, of what we believe in, one to the other. That is why this bill is so important and that is why members opposite should understand why people here feel strongly about it.
We have heard from our constituents. We understand their reality. The reality is that they see their country being destroyed. They see their country being taken apart piece by piece. They see programs that were essential to their identification and to their security as Canadians being undermined. That is the hard reality.
The reason why people are discontented, why there is such anxiety and insecurity is because the props are being taken out. The kind of social contract that we have spent decades trying to build in this country, upon which the market system and the private enterprise system of Canada has been based; the idea that there can be a fundamental framework of security and the government

December 3, 1991
Government Orders
will act as the anchor weight to that is being thrown away. It is being put on the scrap heap by this government.
As soon as you begin to unravel that social contract, as soon as you begin to take that apart, everything else begins to dissolve with it. That is labour fighting management, in hard, conflictual terms. That is when you have region against region and community against community.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: -put people back to work.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
That is the difference.
It strikes me as exceedingly strange. It is almost immoral that a member of this cabinet can sit in his seat and take great pride in an economy where 1.5 million people are out of work. That really is a great economic accomplishment.
That is something to really take great pride in, is it not? Is that not an example of a government that cares? Is that not an example of a government that really knows how to organize an economy, that it will tolerate 1.5 million Canadians unemployed? That is 1.5 million Canadians who no longer make wages, who no longer contribute taxes, who no longer can provide for their families and who must go to food banks. Rather than saying that in regret and sorrow, rather than saying that as a matter of public concern, the minister opposite takes pride in that. He thinks that is an accomplishment.
I say to you that is one reason why the headlines in every newspaper today report that the Conservative government stands at the lowest level in the polls of any government in the last half century and has lost the confidence of all Canadians.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: That's why we have taken reasonable steps to correct the situation.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Oh. Now we
are taking steps to correct the situation. Is it not interesting. Let us look at the steps they have taken. They signed a free trade agreement, so what do we have? The first trade imbalance in 15 years. There is a great important step forward. This was going to be the open
sesame to great trade bounty and we have the first trade deficit in 15 years.
We have the dollar at a level which is exterminating our export industries. We have a situation where 600,000 Canadians go to food banks. When you translate that into hard economic terms, those are human beings who no longer can produce for themselves or their community. As a result they cannot buy things. They cannot buy a fridge, or clothing for their kids at Christmas time. As a result, the retail stores are shutting down. They are firing their employees who will go on reduced unemployment insurance and eventually come off.
What is happening is that the economy is shrinking. Confidence is waning. Demand no longer is there. This government has no answers other than to say that the right steps are being taken. Remarkable. The right steps are being taken.
Around them, the foundations are crumbling, but this brave minister and this brave government march on to their own tune. Unfortunately, nobody in this country is following any longer. Sooner or later their parade is going to come to an end and we are going to get this country back on the tracks again.
The first thing we are going to do is rip up this Bill C-20. That is one of the first things that goes because we are going to have to get back into the business in Canada of investing in proper health care and education. We will never be a strong, productive, competitive nation with a higher education system that is deteriorating and becoming mediocre; that cannot do research or train its students; that is firing professors and cannot buy new books for the library. We will never be a competitive, productive nation if our country begins to destroy its health care system, which gives its own people security.
It is fascinating that the United States, the great paragon of free enterprise, is now debating whether to have a Canadian style medicare system. Why? So that it can become more competitive and productive and have a nation-wide program to bring its own costs into some kind of stability. It is finding that it is paying an awful lot more through its private health insurance plans and therefore reducing its own competitive ability.
December 3, 1991

Government Orders
While they are beginning to look at our plan, we have a government that is destroying it. Once again, this is one of the greatest acts of illogical perversity that has ever been put upon the people of this country.
I do not suppose that anything we say is going to change their minds. I will tell you one thing it is going to do. It is going to hasten the change of a government in this country. It is going to hasten the change back to doing things in a real Canadian way on behalf of all Canadians.
It is going to mean that we are going to get back to deciding what is the priority and I will tell you what the priority is. It is not the illusion that the parliamentary secretary talked about. If this government really wanted to deal with the deficit, then we might have a finance minister brave enough to start recapturing those revenues that they gave away to their big business friends in the last eight years, because that is what Stats Canada said.
Capital gains, write-offs, grants; you name it, you got it. I will tell you the day will come-the day will not come for them because they will not be here any longer- when we will be able to restore some sense of reality to governing in this country. It will be a day to decide who are the winners and the losers. It really is going to come down to a basic battle between a kind of elitist corporate view of the world which is contained in the cabinet rooms of this government, and a democratic view of this world which means that you represent all people and you try to provide the programming, the finances and the economics that represent their concerns.
That is why Bill C-20 is of crucial concern to all of us. It really represents, perhaps as no other piece of legislation has, that difference of view. It represents, perhaps as no other legislation that this government has brought in, the clear demarcation of philosophy and approach as to how to govern this country. It basically points out whose side you are on, and where your interests really lie.
That is why this party is opposed to it and clearly committed to restoring proper federal participation in the support of good education and good health care for this country. That is how we believe we will build a good Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles A. Langlois (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Science and Technology):

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre, instead of speaking to the bill before the House today, has decided to make a very political speech that is full of inaccuracies, false truths and false statements, and I feel it is time to set the record straight.
There are two particular points I wish to address. [English]
The member for Winnipeg South Centre mentioned in his speech that transfer payments to the provinces in the health care program have been reduced. I would like to point out that this is not true. The reality is quite different. The reality is that the increase in transfer payments has grown more slowly in recent years than in the past. This is due to the fact that when this government took power in 1984, the government of which the member for Winnipeg South Centre was a member and a cabinet minister, left it with a deficit of $200 billion. This deficit today is in the area of $400 billion, but the increase is the result of compounded interest of close to $200 billion that has grown on the debt itself. This government has not contributed a black penny to the deficit.
To reimburse the interest on $400 billion you have to pay in the area of $40 billion in interest a year. That is why we had to reduce the growth of the transfer payments. These are the hard facts.

He also said that in 1995-96, the province of Quebec would no longer receive or benefit from federal transfer payments. There again he distorted the facts, because my hon. colleague knows very well that the Government of Quebec decided to take tax points instead of transfer payments. By taking more tax points, as Quebec negotiated with the federal government, it receives less in cash transfer payments. I would like to ask my hon. colleague: When Quebec was asking for more tax points instead of transfer payments and he was a cabinet minister in the government of the day, if he is opposed to that principle today, why did he not express his opposition then and make the case against it that he has in the House today?

December 3, 1991
Government Orders
I say that he should have done so then. It is too late today. Quebec made that choice and the federal government respects it. The federal government will also try to respect it in future, of course, because that is what the province wants.
My hon. colleague from Winnipeg South Centre should tell the House and Quebecers where he was when those discussions were going on.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has taken the occasion to challenge some of the facts. The fact is that Quebec did not opt out of only taking tax transfer points, it still receives cash outlays.
I stand by my record, which is included in the government's own figures, that by the year 1996-97, no longer will there be cash transfers.
I would refer the hon. member to the statements made by his own ministers of health at the meeting in Winnipeg in September where all the health ministers began to say that is the problem.
What he avoids is this question. Perhaps to him it is not an important question, but to many of us it is certainly important. Once the cash transfers disappear, as they will in Quebec in 1996-97, how will the federal government exercise it's responsibility to ensure universality and accessibility of the Canada medicare system? How will it do it? Its answer is: "We will bring in legislation that will give us the right to do it legally". We now know that legally and constitutionally it will be thrown out by the courts. It has been challenged.
Therefore, the federal government's withdrawal from that system will mean that we will end up in a system of different health programs, province by province, region to region. The ones who will pay the most will be the poor provinces which do not have the cash base.
It was not my interpretation. I regret deeply that members opposite are so illiterate. If they had bothered to read the legal opinion that was tabled in front of the committee studying Bill C-20, they would know where the opinion came from. Unfortunately, they have not bothered to do it.
Let us go back to this "deficit issue". This an interesting little debate because Tories love to talk about it. Once again, I will repeat myself because apparently the first or second time they do not quite understand.
Statistics Canada, your agency, run by the Government of Canada, produced a report this spring that said: "What caused the deficit?" It said it was not spending on programs. They have remained the same. What caused it was a loss of revenue because a government reduced and gave away all kinds of revenue it otherwise had by about 20 per cent and high interest rates. What has been the dominant economic policy of the Mulroney government since it has come into power? High interest rates. High dollar, high interest rates, and he said: "We inherited this deficit and it jumped from $125 billion to $400 billion, but we are not responsible. Mea culpa, not me. It could not be us. It went from $125 to $400, but the fact that we have been government for close to eight years is totally irrelevant".
The first four years we had a growth economy. We were averaging 5 per cent, 6 per cent growth a year. It went to 32 separate tax increases at that time. Where did the revenue go? Who did it give the money to? Did it use that revenue of high growth and 32 tax increases to reduce the deficit? Hardly. It is still at $31 billion a year.
What it did in terms of its own brilliant economic analysis, it forced the interest rates up so that what happened is that of course the deficit quadrupled and multiplied in geometric terms. It was a direct consequence of a policy decision taken by this government over the past eight years. That is the reason why that deficit has increased. Therefore-

Mr. Speaker, this week marks the first annual white ribbon campaign, a campaign to help end violence against women through heightening of men's awareness to a problem which takes many forms.
Let the facts speak for themselves. Men make up only 48 per cent of our population, yet are responsible for 90 per cent of the violence. Over 90 per cent of sexual assaults involve female victims. One in four young women under the age of 18 will be abused.
These facts are very real. Women live in fear that the majority of them can expect some form of harassment or sexual violence at some point in their lives. Violence against women is a symptom of deep problems in our society which relate to underlying sexism and stereotyping. Violence against women is not a social problem, it's a crime, as we saw so clearly at Humber College in Etobicoke this last weekend. Only through education can we hope to end such violence. It is time to confront the issue and for all Canadians, female and male, to sjteak out. As we approach the anniversary of the Ecole
Polytechnique, let us remember all victims of violence and their families.

Mr. Speaker, Quebec's new industrial strategy was announced in Montreal yesterday by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Technology, Mr. Gerald Tremblay, in the presence of Premier Robert Bourassa, the leaders of the Conseil du Patronat du Quebec and the Manufacturers' Association, Ghislain Dufour and Richard Le Hir, as well as the presidents of the FTQ and the CNTU, Fernand Daoust and Gerald Larose.
The purpose of the Quebec industrial strategy is to create 200,000 new jobs by the year 2000, thereby bringing the rate of unemployment down to 8 percent. That is a first in North America. Businesses from a given industry will be called upon to join forces or interact to promote job creation and facilitate the emergence of local subcontracting firms. According to Mr. Tremblay, all Quebecers will be invited to contribute to this concerted effort and the success of all is now dependent upon a rapid transition to a value-added economy. The public must take part in the strategy by questioning the generosity of the system and demanding quality products.

The following lay-offs over the last year have resulted in an unemployment rate of 15.2 per cent in my riding of Timmins-Chapleau: Renabie Mines, 190 workers; Dome Mines, 277 workers; Canamax Mines, 99 workers; Pal-mour Mines, 62 workers.

December 3, 1991
Two more lay-offs announced recently will drive the current figures even higher: Abitibi Price, 161 workers; Mike's Supermarkets, 191 workers.
During this holiday season, the only worthy response to this government's handling of the unemployment crisis is: Bah, humbug.]

Mr. Speaker, our brewing industry was supposed to be protected under the free trade agreement, but what we have witnessed after three years of this agreement is that the United States says one thing and does another.
U.S. trade representative Carla Hills has laid down an ultimatum, even before the full GATT council meeting in February, that all discrimination against U.S. beer must end by December 29 or face U.S. duties on all Canadian beer entering the United States. A lot of
Canadian brewery jobs are at stake at Labatt's, Molson's and Moose Head and over $190 million a year in exports to the United States is at stake.
I ask of the government: Will the Canadian government do what it promised under the FTA and support our Canadian brewing industry? Will the Canadian government fight the discriminatory practices of American states against Canadian beer sales in the United States?
Let us tell Carla Hills to snap a cool one of Canada's finest and take a hike.

Mr. Speaker, in mid-October, the Minister of Agriculture spoke about fuel ethanol opportunities to an audience of western farmers and business people.
He indicated that grain or biomass-derived fuel ethanol can be one of Canada's transportation fuel options in the 1990s.
In a few short weeks it will be 1992. Why is it that the United States can take advantage of these market opportunities quickly while Canadian policy is strangled by bureaucratic red tape? The minister should breathe life into a Canadian policy for ethanol production thereby helping farmers, industry and the environment.

Mr. Speaker, the recession is not over in southwestern Ontario.
In Chatham and Kent County, a 400 per cent increase in welfare rates since 1981 and a 30 per cent unemployment rate in the automotive sector alone are signs that the Mulroney-made recession is still here.
Millions of people west of Toronto have been left drowning in a sea of despair, with no regional development program of their own.
I am encouraged by the recent signing of the Canada-Ontario Labour Force Agreement. Chatham, Ontario, and area are prime candidates to receive funding. Skills training is absolutely vital.
The Kent Industrial Training Advisory Committee works with St. Clair College and Wallaceburg's High School was the first in all Ontario to establish a perma-

nent training facility, helping students and the unemployed from basic education to high-tech. I urge the government to put its money where its mouth is and expand support for these and other training facilities to help even more people in this time of economic adjustment.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in the House to join my voice with those of my colleagues who spoke yesterday and today in protest of male violence against women.
Recent events have called on men everywhere to examine their attitudes toward women.

The tragedy at the Ecole Polytechnique took place two years ago. It is a case of terrible violence against women but it is only the most horrible and brutal example. It is time for us to take a more active role and to take on our responsibilities. This white ribbon campaign is an ideal way to make our fellow citizens aware of the need to end violence against women both inside and outside the family.

The white ribbon campaign is rapidly gaining support across Canada. I urge this government to stimulate even greater public awareness by the introduction of education programs.
Through these and other means we will be able to secure a future for Canadian women that is free of violence.
I urge my fellow colleagues to endorse the white ribbon campaign and to take action to decrease the senseless violence against women and I call especially on all aboriginal leaders to do likewise.

Mr. Speaker, the Royal Commission on Reproductive Technology is facing serious allegations of irregularity. Four of the nine commissioners are planning to launch a
lawsuit against the commission and the federal government.
The government interfered with the commission last year when it altered the order in council and appointed two new commissioners. It stripped the commissioners of all responsibility and involvement in the decision-making process in order to vest authority exclusively in the chair.
There are deep concerns that the government is going to disband the commission to avoid the embarrassment of a court case.
New reproductive technologies are advancing ahead of our abilities to understand them and they have deep implications for our society. They are commercializing life and creating the notion of designer babies.
Will the Prime Minister give us his assurance that this commission will not be disbanded simply to avoid embarrassing disclosures?

SPRUCE FALLS POWER & PAPER COMPANY

Mr. Speaker, today, December 3, 1991, is of great historical significance to the northern Ontario towns of Opasatika, Val Rita-Harty, Kapuskasing, Moonbeam and Fauquier. The employees and residents of these towns officially

December 3, 1991
become the majority owners of the Spruce Falls Power & Paper Company, along with Tembec as a minority shareholder.
During the last year, residents of the area have demonstrated tremendous strength and willpower as they were determined to retain 5,000 regional jobs. The loss of these jobs would have been disastrous for the entire region.
Today local investors will start to control their own destiny as the profits will be reinvested in the mill in order to remain competitive in global markets. The $15 million investment by the local people indicates a vote of confidence in the workers' expertise and talent.
I am very proud today to express my sincere gratitude to the men and women who were instrumental in achieving this success by ensuring the future viability of the Spruce Falls Power & Paper Company.

Mr. Speaker, supply and services has awarded $400,000 in research contracts to American universities. One is for planning a model for energy technology, another is on atmospheric oxidizers, another on the validity of lie detectors, and another on interactive teaching technology-
No Canadian universities it is said were capable of doing this work, some of which is of obvious strategic importance.
The question here is not whether contracts should be issued to American universities.
The real question is whether we shall see more and more of this as Canadian universities, deprived of labs and researchers, and increasingly deprived of research and operational funding become increasingly incapable of responding to Canada's competitive needs.

Mr. Speaker, an article in The Gazette last week referred to our constitutional discussions under the heading "All the bickering is among politicians".
It went on to say that relations among the people are surprisingly harmonious. The Gazette does not get much coverage in Alberta, but the theme of its article is just as true there as it is in Montreal.
Thinking Canadians want to keep this country united, but they want other Canadians to understand them and their aspirations. It is no time for us to chase partisan, political points. It is time to listen and to share the opinions expressed by our constituents.
Albertans have shared some very strong feelings with me. They want others to understand us, just as we need to understand them. As MPs, we need to put political considerations aside. Each of us must listen to our constituents in a calm, constructive way. Then we must show them that this House can work, that we can truly represent the views of our constituents and build consensus on it.
The people demand it. The people deserve it. The country is more than worth it.

Mr. Speaker, Thursday, December 5, will mark the official opening of Bendix Avelex Inc. Atlantic Support Division and Atlantic Turbines Inc.

Bendix Avelex is a world class supplier of aerospace and defence equipment. Its Support Services Division
December 3, 1991

provides support of aircraft equipment and accessories for government, commercial and business aircraft. The company is the largest support contractor of its type in Canada. It employs over 20 people and has tremendous growth potential.
Attracting two companies of this calibre to Summer-side is a major accomplishment. It is a beginning, and it is a tribute to the hard work of the Slemon Park Corporation, the P.E.I. Department of Industry and ACOA. I offer my congratulations to all parties and to the two companies involved.

Mr. Speaker, last week the hon. member for South Shore criticized the House of Commons for displaying fake Christmas trees. I could not agree more.

Mr. Speaker, we received the report of the Auditor General of Canada today.

I would like to put my question to the Minister of Finance, but in his absence, I will put it to whoever on that side answers, I guess the acting minister.
The Auditor General's report states that a substantial portion of the annual budgetary deficit is financed by borrowing from pension accounts. Eighteen per cent of the over-all debt, $71 billion, was borrowed in the last years at interest rates below market rates. The government has failed to examine the long-term implications of this practice. I want to ask the government why a study has not been made of this practice.
