speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a great number of factors come into play when one adjusts the management of these funds from the pension funds. The hon. member knows very well that the way it is managed

December 3, 1991
Oral Questions
now stems from legislation that came from this House. He knows also that we are reviewing the Public Service pension legislation, at which time we will look into that.

Mr. Speaker, the government borrowed $71 billion from federal employee pension accounts to finance its deficit. The rates of return on these loans are lower than rates available on the open market. Some people claim that the pension accounts are at risk. Can the minister give the House the assurance that Public Service pension accounts are not at risk and that the government will review this practice, which is not allowed in the private sector? One cannot be sponsor, administrator and trustee. It is against the law. Will the government review this practice?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member will realize that the funds are quite safe, that there is a big difference between a government that cannot go out of business and the private sector, unless of course, that government happens to be the Liberal government which almost did this to Canada. However, in the case of pension fund management, the Auditor General did indicate that there was a difference between the rate of return on those funds and the rate that might have been obtained on the open market. That being said, there are many other factors, including joint management of the funds by the employees and the employer. These are all questions that are being reviewed at this time, as part of our public pension reform.

Mr. Speaker, we do not know the long-term implications of borrowing from pension funds to service the budgetary deficit. There is nothing on the books that we can find to give us some solace at this point.
It is clear from the Auditor General's report that the rate of return of this investment is 1.5 to 2 per cent below market rates, that is the rates the private sector would get in terms of its borrowing. Will the minister assure us that the management of the debt will be improved, that
this government will stop raiding public pension funds to finance its own mismanagement?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the TVeasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:

As I have said and will say again, this is going to be revisited as all other issues of management of the Public Service pension funds over the coming months.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister's old crony, Peter Lesaux, the president of ACOA, said, and I quote: "Illiteracy and rotten weather, that is what is keeping companies out of Cape Breton".
Well, Mr. Speaker, it is not the rotten weather in Cape Breton that is keeping companies out. The Auditor General's report confirms in spades the incompetence of its president and ACOA's mismanagement.
What changes has the minister put in place to adequately monitor and control the action program contribution agreement so that companies like World Communications Network, based in California, will not be able to rip off the Canadian taxpayer?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we all realize that this is just a generality that the hon. gentleman has put forward. There is no specificity, if I might use that word, to it. The totality of his specificities leaves much to be desired.

speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
With respect to ACOA, less than 5 per cent of the projects financed through the action program have been failures. ACOA is there to take risks, to take greater risks let us say than the ordinary commercial banks.
If what the hon. gentleman is proposing is that we apply the same standards and be just as careful as the ordinary commercial banks, we will make no loans in Atlantic Canada whatsoever.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows quite well that the report of the Auditor General seriously indicts ACOA
December 3, 1991

for not adequately evaluating the economic benefit of a project before ACOA makes a financial contribution. That is there very clear for all to see.
What measures will the minister responsible for ACOA put in place to curb abuses like World Communications Network, thereby protecting the Canadian treasury and ensuring that moneys for regional economic development are spent efficiently and used in those areas where they are absolutely needed? What assurances will the minister give the House?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. gentleman wanted to query me about some specific suggestion by the Auditor General, I could deal with it. Of course, in the future we are going to see that they are followed insofar as human abilities permit. There is a slip up occasionally.
With respect to the firm the hon. gentleman is mentioning, I think that firm was located in Cape Breton. We all know that last year we had a study undertaken with reference to the Cape Breton situation and we are following the recommendations of that report of Mr. Braith. In Cape Breton, in particular, we are concentrating more on initiatives put forward by local people and we are much more careful with respect to those who come from outside suggesting that they have some miracle cures to offer for the economic progress of Cape Breton.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. The Auditor General says that the government's plans for cleaning up abandoned toxic waste dumps were doomed to fail. The report says Environment Canada is not up to the task. They have neither the resources nor the staff to identify the sites and clean them up. Why does this important program lack funding? Why is this government putting the health and lives of Canadians at risk?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that what the Auditor General of Canada is saying is that the government intended to
Oral Questions
spend approximately $150 million on cleaning up abandoned sites, and the Auditor General challenges the accuracy of the information we have at this time and feels we have underestimated the work involved. I do not think the Auditor General is challenging the federal government's intentions to act on its responsibility in this area, a responsibility which it shares, I may add, with the provinces.

Clearly what the Auditor General was saying was that there may be the will, but there is certainly not enough money. If there is not the personnel, it just cannot be done and the minister must recognize that.
Today the Auditor General also stated that Revenue Canada Customs is not enforcing the Hazardous Products Act which is supposed to regulate the importation of toxic substances into this country, a very serious issue.
When the Auditor General was asked if this was law breaking, he said this morning: "You could draw that conclusion".
Could the minister explain the ongoing violation of the law concerning importation of toxic substances and could he explain why the health of Canadians is being put at risk every day by importing these unknown substances.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. leader of the New Democratic Party probably knows, there is no evidence whatsoever that one bit of illegal or uncontrolled hazardous material has entered Canada in the last decade or so.
The hon. member also knows that since May 1989, we have enhanced fuel inspection and inspection of other toxic wastes and materials coming into Canada at the borders with random sampling, blitzes, increased inspection tests, fuel contamination examinations and the list goes on, with no evidence whatsoever that any dangerous hazardous material has entered Canada illegally.
On top of that, because of our concern we have gone ahead and signed a memorandum of understanding with the Department of the Environment where we work hand in hand in making sure that operations improve, not only on a yearly basis, but on a daily basis. We have put in new systems, new technology and new people. I

Oral Questions
am satisfied that we are protecting Canada to the best of our abilities.

Mr. Speaker, the minister may be satisfied, but the Auditor General is not satisfied.
The Auditor General says that there is no evidence of Customs actions in enforcing the Hazardous Products Act and in fact a memorandum was sent out which instructs Customs inspectors to release shipments found to contain prohibited or restricted commodities subject to advising Consumer and Corporate Affairs, even though the importation of these products is clearly prohibited.
I would ask the minister to address that issue, because clearly the Auditor General does not agree there is no evidence that these substances are being imported, but quite the opposite.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can again confirm to this House and to Canadians that after random samplings, blitzes and some 1,400 tests which have been taken at the border there is absolutely no evidence that a bit of toxic hazardous illegal material has entered Canada.

You are not checking for it, Otto. No
wonder you are not going to find it.

The hon. member is saying we are not checking for it. I pointed out that in one element only, toxic fuel and toxic waste, there were 1,400 checks. I would like to know from the New Democratic Party what other steps it would want us to take. We have increased the number of staff at the border. We have brought in new systems. We have brought in new technology.
He says you are breaking the law.

We have a memorandum of understanding that has increased our opportunities to protect Canadians from dangerous waste coming into Canada. In the meantime we are continuing our efforts to improve wherever we can on this matter.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister responsible
for DRIE. The minister said he wants specifics with respect to the Auditor General's report and I offer him one, a case singled out by the Auditor General from his own constituency.
The Auditor General reported today that just prior to the last election a door and window manufacturer in St. John's, Newfoundland received a $5.2 million non-repayable grant from ACOA just 30 days after its application was filed with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. The grant in question was made within a 30-day period, notwithstanding the fact that DRIE had raised serious questions about the company's operations and about the new company's effect on existing window manufacturers in St. John's.
My question to the minister responsible for ACOA is the following: Why were all the normal rules scuttled, during a pre-election period, in the minister's own backyard?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the one hand we have the member opposite suggesting ACOA is inefficient. On the other hand, we have another member getting up and suggesting there is tremendous efficiency in ACOA. Which is it?
As a matter of fact I was not the minister responsible for ACOA at the time of the last election.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Apparently it took ACOA 210 days to review and approve this particular application, 210 days. If I had known about it, it would have been done one heck of a lot quicker than that, supposing that it met the criteria.
In addition, it was recommended for approval by the project review committee. There is a project review committee. That company is operating successfully with 50 full-time employees. The hon. member should be congratulating ACOA on the support it gave in this particular instance.

Mr. Speaker, the minister's attempt at humour will not disguise the fact that during an election campaign after only 30 days a $5.2 million non-repayable gift-grant was given to a company in the minister's own backyard. It was given at a time when the rules provided for a grant of up to $20 million under a so-called fast program when today
December 3, 1991

the rule allows only for a loan of up to $500,000. Why the giveaways during an election and today only loans?
How is the minister of ACOA going to investigate the irregularities pointed out in the Auditor General's report in his own constituency? Where is the conflict of interests here and how can Canadians get an honest accounting for their tax dollars?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we always very much enjoy the hon. gentleman's performances. I am sure we do on this occasion, but he is dealing with a company that has been successful and where the criticism of the Auditor General is technical in nature.
There was a change of ownership in connection with the application. A considerable period went by between the original application and the later application that was approved. There had been a change of ownership in the meantime which our officials thought strengthened the company. That was not brought to the minister's attention. This is the nature of the criticism of the Auditor General.
As I said earlier, it took ACOA 210 days to review and approve it. There was no rushing of this approval through. It has been a success and 50 persons in Newfoundland are now working who might not otherwise have been working. Why the criticism by the hon. gentleman opposite?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment. In his report last year, the Auditor General asked the government to develop ways for reporting to Parliament on how it was meeting its environmental responsibilities. A year later the result, to quote from the Auditor General's report tabled today, is:
(-) No such clarification has yet been made.
In short, the minister has done nothing in a year. My question is: Why this disdain, this contempt for the Parliament of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the hon. member for LaSalle-Emard likes to get excited about such ques-
Oral Questions
tions. I think that if he took a little time to analyse Canada's green plan, he would see that the government made a commitment in that plan to various environmental measuring and reporting mechanisms. We will indeed report to the Parliament of Canada in 1992. If he took the time to read the whole Auditor General's report, I am not sure, but I think that the Auditor General also admits that we will report to Parliament using that mechanism.

Mr. Speaker, the Auditor General has specifically condemned this minister as a do-nothing minister. The previous Minister of the Environment promised achievement dates for the green plan. This minister backed off. The previous Minister of the Environment promised environmental assessment policy. This minister backed off.
Under this minister the department has been found guilty of blocking the legitimate requests of Canadians under the Access to Information Act, and now the Auditor General has said that under this minister the government is shirking its responsibility to Parliament.
My question is: Where does this minister get off with blocking the public's right to know?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean J. Charest (Minister of the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that once Canadians get beyond the rhetoric and all the showmanship of the hon. member from Lasalle-Emard they will find that this government committed itself to a $3 billion green plan over six years. We proceeded to implement that green plan with due diligence.
We announced $100 million, for example, for the Fraser River initiative. We announced $100 million for an Arctic environment strategy under the green plan. We announced $100 million under forestry for development of sustainable forests. We announced $250 million for an initiative for sewage for native people. We announced $25 million for an initiative in drinking water for people. We announced $50 million for more research in the area of-
More, more.

Mr. Speaker, the government's new native agenda promised to improve socio-economic conditions for aboriginal peoples in this country.
My question is therefore to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Today the Auditor General's report shows that his department knew that it had a backlog of over 10,000 housing units. It knew that 72 per cent of the housing stock did not even come up to code, and yet it still did nothing about it.
When is the minister of Indian affairs going to face up to the crisis in native housing in this country and do something positive about it?

Hun. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)): Mr. Speaker, my colleague should recognize that this government has made a very determined commitment, with a very specific agenda, to improving the condition of native communities.
We are developing a housing policy in consultation with native groups. My hon. colleague should admit that we develop those policies in close cooperation with the communities in order to improve the programs and make them more effective.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
Today's report of the Auditor General shows that reinstatements under Bill C-31 have been 50 per cent higher than the Department of Indian Affairs predicted in 1985. Aboriginal groups are saying: "We told you so".
Despite the assurance that no band would suffer from this sudden influx of native women and children, the department made no plans to house them properly. My question is very simple: Why not? Why have proper plans not been made to house these people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think that my hon. colleague should recognize that annual investments of $120 million to $140 million do constitute real and specific commitments to providing housing assistance to native communities.
We are aware of the fact that more is required under Bill C-31. As a matter of fact, the policy is being reviewed. I must say that at present, funds made available to native people allow 3,000 new houses to be built each year, and the renovation of another 3,000 to 4,000 houses every year on top of that. I think those are very concrete and specific commitments.
As regards the problem with sewers and sanitary conditions these communities are faced with, very specific commitments were made on that too. As my colleague the Minister of the Environment mentioned earlier, we will be spending $250 million over the next six years on sewers and another 25 million on drinking water.
Mr. Speaker, these are firm commitments.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
The Auditor General today indicates that the Department of Transport, the Minister of Transport and indeed the entire cabinet approved a 42-year lease for the construction of a hotel at Halifax International Airport without any evidence that the rooms were needed or that the developer had the financing in place to complete this project.
I ask the minister: if the money was not in place and the rooms were not needed, what exactly were the criteria used by the minister to advise his cabinet to approve this project?

Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member and all members of this
December 3, 1991

House that most of the risk has been borne by the lessee. My department did rely on the financial industry's risk assessment because it was this group, not the department, that invested the risk capital in the development.
I think at the time of the examination of this proposal that all matters were in good standing and we approved it because we thought it was a good investment for the region.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
As a result of this government's bungling we now have a half-finished concrete bunker attached to Halifax International Airport.
My question to the minister is this: Is it now the government's intention to fund the completion of this hotel, or will it dip further into taxpayers' pockets to tear down this latest monument to the minister's cabinet's and his colleagues' incompetence?

Mr. Speaker, the matter is now being examined first of all by the trustee and other financial interests.
We want this hotel to be completed, and as we get through the present proceedings we will make sure that this hotel is completed to the satisfaction of the customers in the area because we think that it is a good addition economically speaking for the region.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister of industry.
Farmers and fishermen are asking for money and the government always says that it has no money. Can the minister give us an explanation of why his department gave $26 million out of the DIPP fund to companies that did not even ask for the money?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Tbade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. minister who has been a minister of industry knows that there is a very vigorous requirement for companies to go through in getting access to those funds.
That program is a good program. It provides very good support for science and technology and for research and development, particularly in high-tech sectors that need this sort of financing. He knows perfectly well that there
Oral Questions
is a very rigorous set of approvals required in order to get access to those moneys.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is this: In his report published today, the Auditor General said that at the end of the year, the minister's department gave $28 million to firms which had not even asked for funding. Why is there money for the government's friends, when there is none for the farmers and fishermen of this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me be quite clear to the hon. Leader of the Opposition. There are situations wherein the department discusses with the industry whether or not there should be an access to funds in one year or another in order to meet the requirements that both the industry and the government agree are to be met.
It is under those circumstances that this type of agreement is entered into.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. Yesterday, the U.S. government announced that the preferential rate offered by Hydro-Quebec to Norsk-Hydro constitutes an unfair subsidy. A countervailing duty of 33 per cent will be imposed on magnesium exports to the United States. My question is this: Is this government finally prepared to admit its free trade agreement gives us no protection against the protectionist policies of the United States? And does this government intend to forget about Quebec's interests, as it is now doing at GATT?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me be very clear to the hon. member.
Under the free trade agreement either side can challenge the other side if they feel that there is a subsidy, as we have done on a number of occasions with the Americans and as they have done here.

December 3, 1991
Oral Questions
We disagree that there is a subsidy in this. We are working with the province and with the industry to make sure that we put the strongest possible case forward. We also have challenged the American companies as to whether they have standing, whether they have a right to put the case forward as has been done, and we are challenging this under the GATT.
Finally let me say that under the rules of the free trade agreement-and let me remind my hon. friend that this is a preliminary determination-if the ultimate decision is something that we disagree with we have the right under the free trade agreement to take the matter to a bi-national panel dispute settlement mechanism in order to challenge that. That was not the case prior to the free trade agreement.

Mr. Speaker, obviously we are not getting the answer that the government knows is the real answer, that the free trade agreement is not working in Canada's interest. It has not worked in British Columbia with softwood lumber. It has not worked in Quebec. It is not working at all.
I would like the minister to respond exactly and definitely. What is he going to do? What is he going to tell the companies? We are not just talking about one company here but other companies, aluminium companies that can be faced with the same problem. Quebec and its development can be seriously handicapped.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me say to my friend that his bluster does not add anything to the understanding of people about that particular issue.
I have indicated very clearly that we are going to take the strongest possible position in working with the province and with the industry to make sure that our interests are upheld in this particular case. We are also challenging the matter under the GATT, whether the company has the legitimacy to put this case forward.
Finally, as I said, we have the right under the free trade agreement which we have not had before and which is not effective under the GATT, to take a matter to a dispute settlement mechanism panel to ensure that our rights are upheld.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.
The original ACOA mandate was for $1 billion, subsequently extended over seven years, to help achieve regional development in Atlantic Canada that would not otherwise occur without federal assistance.
I am led to understand that portions of these annual budgets are subject to lapsing of funds which are not expended by the end of the fiscal year, thus leading in some cases to unused ACOA money or, perhaps more often and more seriously, to excessive efforts at finding ways to spend the money before it lapses. Either way the concept of lapsing funds would seem to distort ACOA's purposes within artificial budget boundaries.
My question is this: Can a mechanism not be found to ensure that ACOA's funds do not lapse at budget year-end but rather are allowed to accumulate in the subsequent year for application to justifiable projects as they are created?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are going to have some lapsing members opposite when the next election comes.
Call the election right now.

speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Don't tempt me. With reference to the question of lapsing funds, ACOA's track record is actually quite good with respect to that. Every department has the problem of lapsing funds if they do not spend the moneys voted to them during the year. Of course they cannot always tell how much they will be spending. It depends upon the demand in the action program for loans and the like.
Of the $277 million allocated last year for grants and contributions, we cash managed those funds within less than $5 million. Only $5 million lapsed, which was less than 2 per cent. The hon. gentleman does not need to worry about ACOA. If we lapse any funds we will see that they are spent in Atlantic Canada in any event the following year.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
A gross miscarriage of justice has occurred in Brazil and two Canadians are involved. On appeal, Christine Lamont and David Spencer have had their sentences increased to 28 years each for their alleged participation in a highly publicized Brazilian kidnapping, though much of the evidence points to their innocence.
The minister has refused to help these Canadians. This sentence is harsher than a murder sentence in Canada and the sentence is absolutely preposterous. When will the minister recognize the injustice of this case and take immediate steps to request their expulsion from Brazil?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have pointed out before, the department and our consular services have been very active in assisting this couple in any way that they can. They have also monitored the whole legal process that has been used.
In my view the sentence is excessive and I am going to explore the ruling from the Court of Appeal in Brazil. When I have done that I will be happy to review whether there is anything further that can be done.
Having said that, let me remind the member that I have personally reviewed this case on two occasions. We are dealing with two mature adult Canadians. She is 31. He is 29. They have been found guilty of kidnapping, conspiracy and resisting arrest. Both entered Brazil on fraudulent Canadian passports. All the co-defendants received the same sentence, and they have not been tortured as some reports have alleged.
I have asked my officials to review the circumstances surrounding the sentencing, but those are the facts.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the minister.
Oral Questions
The minister has been making a lot of speeches about defending human rights abroad. I want to ask her: Is it not time to start defending the human rights of Canadians, of our own citizens?
Clearly under Brazilian law a foreign national does not have the same right as a Brazilian national to ask for an appeal or to ask for parole. Is that not a denial of the rights of Miss Lamont and Mr. Spencer?
I want to ask the minister: When is she going to take her fundamental responsibility to represent the interests of Canadians abroad and ask the Brazilian government for the right of expulsion, which is what the Brazilian judge said the minister should do?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it strikes me that the hon. member takes to shouting when he knows he does not have a substantive case.
I have responded to the first question by saying that I think the sentence is a severe one and I intend to review the appeal. Surely that is my responsibility. That is what I plan to do, but that does not alter the fundamental facts of the case which include the fact that the other co-conspirators were given the same sentence.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State (Employment and Immigration). Mr. Petar Zilic, a resident of Saint-Leonard who is originally from Croatia, was informed that his parents had been tortured and killed in the village of their birth, which has now been destroyed. Fearing for their lives, the rest of his family has fled, leaving behind important documents such as their passports and other identification. Could the minister introduce some exceptional measures to help Mr. Zilic, and others like him, bring their families who are living in terror to this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to remind hon. members that our immigration procedures provide for certain

December 3, 1991
Oral Questions
extraordinary measures, and that we respect people on an individual basis, with a constant focus on a humanitarian approach.
As for the specific case that was just described, I will submit your request to the responsible minister, and we will report back at the appropriate time.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a telephone call to the office of the minister of immigration and yesterday afternoon to the Minister of State for Immigration, my office was told that without identification there would be little chance for Mr. Zilic to get his family to join him in Canada. speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister of State (Employment and Immigration) and Minister of State (Seniors)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Seniors); Minister of State (Employment and Immigration)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at the risk of repeating myself, every case is dealt with individually under Canada's Immigration Act and we will do what is necessary to comply with our law.

Mr. Garth Tbrner (Halton

Peel): Mr. Speaker, yesterday the foreign minister told this House that Canada would commit troops to peacekeeping duties in Croatia. My constituents of Croatian descent very much appreciate that, but they also want Canada to recognize Croatian independence, just as we granted it this week to Ukraine.
My question is this: What criteria does Croatia have to meet in order to gain Canada's blessing as a sovereign state?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's ongoing interest in this matter. As I said before, there are a great many differences between the situation in Ukraine and the situation in Croatia.
The first thing we are looking for in Croatia and in other parts of Yugoslavia is an end to the violence within the context of a negotiated comprehensive settlement. This is the only way we see that this obscene violence can be brought to an end.
Second is the protection of minorities. Third is agreed borders. We will not recognize borders that are taken by force. Fourth is respect for human rights and other CSCE principles.
I should point out that when the referendums were taken in Croatia and Slovenia under the Brioni agreement, both republics agreed to a three month moratorium before asking for independence.
We are now in a situation where the key to independence is to ending the violence and to have all the parties negotiate in good faith. We have been urging them to do that for some months through every forum that is available to us.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister responsible for ACOA.
The Auditor General's report identifies significant instances where ACOA officials failed to inform the minister of changes to proposals, changes to recommendations not to proceed with a project and advanced millions of dollars to companies that did not meet funding guidelines.
This is an incredible situation. I am asking the minister: Will he now admit that the agency is out of control and without direction? Will he indicate to the House what steps he intends to take to fix these obvious problems with ACOA?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member does not do this House or the country any service by such ridiculous general statements and accusations.
ACOA is not out of control. ACOA is dealing with hundreds and thousands of applications every year. In a few instances certain technical points have been missed by a project officer or whatever, none the cause of any

serious losses to ACOA. So I can only say the hon. gentleman is grossly exaggerating and doing a disservice.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to stand in the House and address the whole question of Bill C-20.
I will attempt to show that it is a brutal and insensitive piece of legislation. It is divisive.

I would go even further. It is tearing the country apart. It is misleading. It is inadequate legislation. It simply will not work. It will never ever be accepted.

Before I get into those particular details to prove those particular points, I just want to summarize very quickly the contents of the bill to remind viewers and my colleagues that it deals with the capping and the freezing of transfers to provinces in health, education, social assistance in terms of three provinces and increases to the unemployment insurance premiums as well as to the freezing of the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act. Those revenues would normally go to the provinces.
I also want to make the next point which I think is very important. We are talking about $36 billion in transfers if one looks at cash and tax points. That is a great deal of money. It is an amount of money that our provinces and
our territories really need in order to carry on everyday life in terms of government and in order to ensure that Canadian citizens, wherever they happen to live, get the kinds of programs to which they are entitled.
They are talking about $24 billion in cash, $12 billion in tax transfer points and we are talking with respect to Established Programs Financing, that is funding for health and education in the neighbourhood of $20 billion. With respect to equalization, it is approximately $8 billion and with regard to Canada Assistance, it is about $6 billion, that is the social assistance programs. Of course, there are other categories that may amount to close to $3 billion. As I indicated previously, it is a lot of money.
I started by saying that this was not appropriate legislation at this particular point in time. One would expect that from a member of the opposition, but let me share with you some statements that have been made by others.
There is a press release from the Government of Canada, the National Council of Welfare, entitled "Cash payments for medicare and higher education in jeopardy". I did not say that. The National Council of Welfare and the Government of Canada said that.
I have another communique. This time, it is from the Canada Council on Social Development. What does it say? "Federal budget may destroy Canada's social system". This was said by the Canada Council on Social Development.
Here is yet another in a Citizen article, a recent one: "Group's fear of breakdown of national programs". There is a journalist who is looking at it after having talked to people, after having studied this situation, and that is the judgment that is rendered.
I will refer, finally, to one more article from The Globe and Mail dated November 28, 1991. It is entitled Plan to preserve medicare risky under law MPs are told. What has happened here? Basically, the government has noticed that it will no longer be transferring dollars, that is cash, to provinces for health and education, particularly for health.
What it has done is within that particular bill it has a section that intends to withhold other kinds of payments in the event that the provinces do not respond to the standards that are expected of the federal government.
December 3, 1991

What kinds of hold-outs could there be? What kinds of demands might there be? The federal government might attack the equalization payments which are in the neighbourhood of $8.4 billion. It might go to territorial financing which is in excess of $1 billion. It might attack grants in lieu of taxes to provincial and municipal governments by the federal government. These amount to $344 million. They could in fact if they chose go to public utilities, income tax, transfer payments, and that represents $260 million, or statutory subsidies to the oldest kind of transfer payment in the neighbourhood of $36 million. The government could in fact attack the Canada Assistance Plan, over $6 billion, or the crop insurance program, $297 million. I think it is $207 million in the current year.
These are the kinds of programs that the government could hold back payments on and here are some others. The government could in fact go to the official languages and education program where there was $243 million that was given to provinces last year, or miscellaneous health and welfare which amounted to $170 million, or the young offenders' services for $158 million, or justice transfers for $77 million, and finally transfers in the domain of transportation for $69 million.
This is what this bill could in fact lead the government to do. That is if the provinces were not to use the funds that they get, the tax transfer points that they get, in the way the federal government wanted them to do so.
Therefore we have students, young offenders, farmers, business people, women, and many many others who could in fact be penalized as a result of a provincial government's inability or unwillingness to respond to the criteria and the standards that are set by the federal government with regard to the utilization of health care funds.
I started off by saying that I considered this particular bill, C-20, to be brutal and insensitive. Why did I say that? I think it ignores the realities of today. I have spoken before as have many of my colleagues about the poor in this nation, over 5 million at this very moment who are living at or below the level of poverty, most of whom are women, and many of whom are senior citizens, and over 1 million of whom are children. I talked about
Government Orders
the people receiving social assistance, 2 million as we speak right now, about the people who would be fed par des banques alimentaires, 1.8 million people this year in Canada, almost 1.5 million people who in fact are receiving unemployment insurance. The list goes on and on and on.
Why brutal and insensitive? Because which of those particular people in those groups will be receiving any particular assistance from this kind of legislation? Not one single one.
What else will happen? The contributing provinces, provinces such as Ontario, British Columbia, and Alberta, which contribute funds to the rest of Canada in order to even out the unevenness in terms of wealth so that other Canadians can receive basic services and health, education, social assistance, and what have you so that the quality of life is more or less the same, are suffering too. They are suffering too. Yet they have been capped with respect to social assistance expenditures.
How does that make them feel? On the one hand they have paid off huge sums of money. On the other hand they are being capped additionally. The resentment is growing not only in these provinces but it is creating two classes of people, that class which contributes, the class which receives, and there is growing tension and conflict. As well it is leading to the small and those who are weaker economically becoming even weaker, that is they are not able to offer the essentials of the quality of life.
There will be additional suffering.

Unfortunately, this bill does absolutely nothing for these people, whether we are talking about the poor, people who get their food from food banks, the unemployed or people on welfare.

I also said that this particular bill was divisive. Yes, it is. It is increasingly so because some of our wealthier provinces are able to spend more in spite of the fact that they are having difficult times, for example in their hospitals or their post-secondary educational institutions, so we are establishing different classes of colleges and universities. How would you feel, Mr. Speaker, how would we all feel if our particular universities and

December 3, 1991
Government Orders
colleges in our provinces could not offer the same kinds of quality programs that are offered elsewhere.
There is province against province, university against university, college against college, region against region, and I have already indicated that Ontario, B.C., and Alberta sometimes feel as if they are against the rest of Canada.

I think it is too bad we are seeing region against region, that some institutions are being neglected by the federal government in terms of funding and are no longer able to provide the services they want to provide, such as health care, education and social assistance. We are creating one class of people who are more or less well off and another class of people who are definitely not well off, and I think the gap between the two is growing at an alarming rate.

I also said initially that this particular bill was misleading. Why did I say it was misleading? There is a very strong suggestion on the part of government that it is being done to control the deficit and the debt. We heard it again today. We know that the deficit is in the neighbourhood of $30 billion. No one is happy about that. We know that the debt is in excess of $400 billion. Certainly we are saddened by that. What is really extremely offensive is that the government suggests that it is at that particular height size, call it what you will, level, because of the deficit and the debt that it inherited from the previous administration.
I am sorry, that is not true. I have a signed letter from the former Minister of Finance, the Minister for International Trade, indicating that the debt in the year in which the government took over power was less than $168 billion. Factor in the interest rates since then and there is no way that it built up to $400 billion. I have done it, I have had others do it. I guess it is a kind of misleading statement, that effort to try to lay the blame on others rather than to say: "Look, we have made some mistakes, here are some of them, here is what we are trying to do in order to correct them".
It is misleading because what will this particular bill do? What have previous cuts done to reduce the deficit and the debt? Canadians see no evidence of it. They
have had well over 30 tax increases, including the hated goods and services tax. They are paying more than ever before. The middle class is being bludgeoned, the poor are even poorer, and those at the top of the salary scale are getting away with more and more. People out there are saying: When is it going to stop?
They would not be nearly as offended if they could see progress being made, if they could see the deficit being lowered, the debt being lowered, if they could see their jobs being secure, their future in terms of pensions being realized-now they worry as to whether or not they will ever be able to get them-see their sons and daughters with opportunities for a good education, for a meaningful job where they will be able to develop their total talent and contribute fully to this country, indeed the whole world. Then they would be less alarmed, then they would be less offended.

Unfortunately, this bill does too little. It gives every indication that it will do something to reduce the deficit and the debt but, unfortunately, that is not the case. There is no evidence to support that claim. If we look at all the increases we have had since 1984-and I believe it was 34-we have not made any headway. We have slipped back. Take, for instance, the debt as a percentage of the Gross National Product. This ratio has changed drastically since 1984. There has been negative growth, which does nothing for us, for Parliament, for government or the country.

My final point when I first introduced the bill in order to address it was it will not work. Why will it not work? Already we know it is being contested, and that is a very poor start for any piece of legislation. We know that it will create further animosity. I pointed out that the provinces are being capped, they are not happy because they are suffering. Look at the province of Ontario, the number of bankruptcies, the number of unemployed, the number of people on social assistance, and somehow this capping suggests to Ontario, to B.C. or to Alberta that they have it good.
They do not have it good. They are having serious difficulties, as is the rest of Canada. What will happen? There will be additional intolerance, animosity and anger that will be generated as a result of this particular
December 3, 1991

treatment. What will our young people say when they know full well that there will be no more dollars for health as their parents get older or for themselves as they reach the age when they need more medical care? As they want to go on to college and university, they see that the opportunities are slipping for an education or jobs or for a meaningful future. How will they respond? How could they possibly contribute fully?
Surely we all sense the great disappointment not only in this piece of legislation but in many other decisions that have been taken which limit the quality of life for our citizens throughout Canada whether we speak of health care, education, social assistance or a number of other areas.

As I said when I started my speech, I wish I were wrong. I wish I were wrong about my predictions that this bill will not work, will not produce the results it was intended to produce, at least the ones the government said it was intended to produce, in other words, reduce the deficit and the debt and try and establish a much sounder system than the one we have today, in order to put our economy on a sound footing, so that we can establish those social programs that respond to the needs of Canadians. Unfortunately, that is not the case.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I simply wish to repeat that I think it is too bad that this bill does not address the real problems of Canadians today. I find this bill harsh and insensitive, even improper; it will foster more division. It offers too little and it will not work at all. It tries to give the impression that cuts will improve Canadians' economic situation, although that is not so.
I will complete my speech with one remark. We heard it in the House of Commons yesterday, and in the Citizen today, there is an article which says:

"Tighten Belts, MP Tells Premiers". I suppose that one of the more offensive things that the government has done is to suggest that it has been controlling the expenditures of the federal government when we all know that it has been putting them off on the backs of
Government Orders
the provinces and the territories and every single man and woman who is paying taxes.
I said it before and I want to say it again. It is very easy to control one's expenses when you give them to someone else. I have debts and if I were able to walk around and share them with my colleagues here in the House I would walk out of the House debt free. I expect I would get some resistance by the way. But that is what has happened.
The government says it has controlled the expenditures in the neighbourhood of 3 per cent. That is no wonder. It has given all of its expenses to the provincial governments and then on to the hospitals, the universities, the colleges and then to the students and the patients and what have you.
I see this kind of statement: "Tighten Belts, MP Tells Premiers" as misleading. That is the kindest word that comes to mind and I could think of others that are much less kind. It does not tell the whole truth. I think it is part of the malaise that exists in our country today and that is why the citizen out there is less than confident about political parties and politicians. That is why the citizen out there really wants a fundamental change, a change which will lead to fierce debate about the ideas and the issues. I am sure Canadians throughout the nation welcome that. They also want accurate information so that they can make the judgments as to who is right and who is wrong.
I rest my case. I say that Bill C-20 is regressive. It will not fulfil the objectives that the government stated or left unstated. It will not curb the deficit or the debt. It will disappoint a lot of people: the poor, the unemployed, the people who have to go to food banks, those who are on social assistance, and all of those other Canadians who are dependent or will be dependent upon medical treatment. It will also disappoint those who will want an education, a better job and a retirement with some dignity.

I would be so pleased if the government would consider the points made by my colleagues and me with a view to changing some aspects of the bill and maybe government policy as well.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate my colleague for St. Boniface on an excellent presentation. I would like to build on what my colleague was discussing.
The reason why Bill C-20 was introduced was to allow the government to deal with its budget of February 26, 1991. I would like to talk about one segment of that particular budget. It deals with the transfer payments to the provinces in the area of post-secondary education.
If the government follows its plan there will be no transfer payments to the provinces in both health care and post-secondary education by the year 2004.
This is very alarming. In a way it is in contradiction with what the government is presently talking about in its constitutional proposals, in particular the proposals that deal with learning and our ability to compete internationally.
It is unfair for the federal government on one hand to talk about the importance of education and on the other hand cut transfer payments. The provinces on their own as well as the municipalities and the school boards cannot carry on with the existing workload without some federal government support.
"There has been a cut of $485 million from the 1991 educational budget. When you look at the federal government training and educational contributions it has dropped by 4.6 per cent. Compare that with the amount of increase in government spending which is in the amount of 4.3 per cent. On one hand you have the spending in certain areas having been increased while on the other hand when it comes to education and spending on learning and training, it has decreased.
Between 1984 and 1986 the federal government slashed approximately $9.5 billion in transfer payments to the provinces. As we move forward there seems to be less and less commitment by the federal government toward education and the provinces.
While there has been a decrease in funding for education, we see the student costs have been on the rise. Looking at post-secondary education, Statistic Canada reports that in the province of Ontario alone the tuition fees have increased by approximately 53.5 per cent between 1983-84 and 1990-91. Where there has been an increase in tuition fees and costs of education
there has been a decrease in federal contributions toward post-secondary education.
Consider the cost of student accommodation across Canada. In my riding alone the cost of residence fees has increased between 40.6 and 176 per cent since 1984-85. For example, six years ago a room in residence at one of the two universities used to rent for somewhere between $1,127 and $1,326 a year. Now they are rented at a cost of approximately $1,600 to $3,600. My colleague from Newfoundland says "incredible".
On top of the cost of living increases, the federal government has introduced a 3 per cent tax on student loans and applied the GST to books. This has added at least a few hundred dollars to many students' financial burden and has hit hardest those of middle or low income.
The government has decreased its funding to education, and that is extremely clear in Bill C-20 with its implications. You must look at the area of research and development, for example, and what the government said in 1984 and what has happened since then. In 1984 the government made a commitment to double the percentage of the gross domestic product spent on research and development. But what has happened, in fact, is the amount of money spent on research and development has decreased from 1.42 per cent in 1985 to 1.36 per cent in 1990.
So that tells us as we move into the 20th century that the federal government is investing less and less in the area of research and development and education.
We are going to be faced with an alarming situation over the next few years. By the year 2030, one in every four Canadians will be a senior citizen, compared to one in every ten now. By the end of the century, senior citizens will represent approximately 13 per cent of the population and youth will represent about 9.4 per cent. The reason why I say this is because I want you to know that our tax base is shrinking as a result of the fact that we have a lot less people now who are paying taxes than we used to have in the past and we will have even less in the future than we have right now.
Because of this shrinkage in the tax base, we are going to see more pressure on the infrastructures such as our health care system and our social welfare system. Those seniors will need more care and assistance. As a result of

that the government will have to look at ways to generate more revenue.
In my view, one way is to invest in the areas of education and research and development, rather than cutting down. I will elaborate on that by mentioning only the question of productivity in Canada.
If we look at the productivity of Canada's work force, we find that it has lagged behind the other economically advanced countries. A high percentage of our work force, as you know, is illiterate to some degree and unable to cope with new technology. The problem is especially serious in light of the current shift in world trade. Resource commodities, which are Canada's economic mainstay, are being replaced by information and knowledge-intensive goods.
Speaking again about productivity in terms of our work force, we compare Canada's productivity growth with that of the G-7 countries. We score very miserably in key sector of international competitiveness. For example, in 1990 Canada ranked well below the middle among 23 countries surveyed by the World Economic Forum. The forum looked at factors such as international orientation, managerial initiative and the quantity of skilled labour.
International comparisons in general have shown that we are investing enough to remain competitive as long as the skills our students learn are relevant. Obviously, that investment is not giving us the return that we are expecting from it.
The reason I say that is because nearly 40 per cent of the Canadian population has difficulty reading, writing and doing basic math tasks. In comparison, Japan's rate of illiteracy has been estimated to be less than 1 per cent, in West Germany it is less than 4 per cent and in the United Kingdom it is less than 6 per cent.
Obviously we have a situation where national attention is required if we are to really deal with the questions of productivity, reducing the deficit and competing internationally.
That supports the fact that the federal government should not be making cuts in the areas of research and development, training and education; it should be investing in them.
A 1990 study released by the Conference Board of Canada has found that illiteracy hinders companies from
Government Orders
bringing in new technology, such as computer or high-tech equipment. That study found-and my colleague from Broadview-Greenwood is carefully listening to this as the critic for small business-that almost one-third of the 626 companies surveyed said that illiteracy had significantly slowed down work or caused quality control problems because workers could not understand instructions.
Also, the Canadian Business Task Force on Illiteracy estimates that the cost to our Canadian society is approximately $10 billion a year and the cost to business itself is approximately $4 billion a year. The government is really barking up the wrong tree.
We are cutting back in areas which in my view we should be investing in more. We are cutting back in those areas thinking that we will reduce and control the deficit. That is similar to someone who might, as I said many times before, sell the furniture in order to pay the rent. The other way should be true. The government should set up a fairly aggressive strategy in terms of investing and call it investment. Do not call it expenditure because it is not an expenditure. Call it an investment and move on.
There are other areas where the government is not investing. Those areas are adult training and education, as I mentioned before, but also I want to just mention the question of training. The government seems to be talking about it quite a bit lately.
There is an alarming situation where the average Canadian worker participated in 6.7 hours of formal training in 1988. By contrast an Australian worker received 17 hours, a Swede received 170 hours, and a Japanese 200 hours annually in terms of training. We should compare ourselves to other countries around the world in the area of investment in training. This is a shocking figure where the government is not investing in the training of the work force.
That very same work force is going to move us into the next century and help us to be competitive internationally. It is going to provide the taxes and the revenues that our government will need in order to support our needy population.
Also, it is really interesting that only one-third of Canadian companies provide any training to employees at all. Of course they cannot provide enough training to

Government Orders
employees because there is not enough investment on the part of the government. There are not enough incentives on the part of the government. There is not enough involvement on the part of the government in the area of training. Yes, there are certain programs out there, but those programs are not doing enough. Those programs are not doing the job.
In the Conference Board survey, 75 per cent of companies reported basic problems with literacy. The government will invest some money in the area of literacy over the next five years and some of my colleagues mentioned that the amount of money that is spent literally comes to a few dollars per illiterate. That certainly is not enough investment in the area of illiteracy.
What we have to do is invest more in the area of education and not less. Look for instance at what we spend on adult training or teaching. We spend approximately $5 billion and that is roughly about one-eighth of the amount invested in formal education. But when we are facing other countries, we see that they are increasing their investment on an annual basis, not reducing it.
For example, Germany has increased its expenditures on training by 45 per cent in the last three years. Germany has acknowledged that to move into the 21st century, it has to do something really drastic. It has acknowledged that the international barriers to world trade have been removed. It has acknowledged that the number one country in the world will be the one that deals with the question of education aggressively, that treats education as a priority, and treats training as a priority, so it is investing more.
Japan for example is also increasing its spending on an annual basis at an incredible rate. I do not have the figures, but I presume they are doing more there than we are here in Canada.
Look at this and compare it to what our experts in our government are telling us. I want to look at just the Department of Employment and Immigration that rightly predicts that many of the low-skill jobs in the next century will simply disappear. We will not have any more jobs that an unskilled individual can do. The reasons for that are automation, globalization of trade, and the
growing importance of the service sector, which is just beginning. There is a shift and we are losing a lot of our industry that used to use primitive technology. They are simply disappearing off the map and are replaced with industry that is using high-tech equipment. But when you use high-tech equipment you need more or less high-tech employees to be able to work on that equipment and read the instructions.
Obviously, with the quality of workers that we have now they cannot do it on their own. They need the support of the government. They need investment on the part of the government so they can catch up and move on into the next century, fully equipped with the knowledge that they need.
The reason I brought those figures to your attention is to tell you that Bill C-20 in a way does put a cap on and gives the wrong signal, not to the provinces or the universities or the municipalities, but to society as a whole. We are telling society that we have a difficult situation here. We do not have the money and we are not going to do anything about it.
In my view, that is the wrong approach.
Even if we have to mortgage the House of Commons, the government should do it in order to invest in areas such as education, training and combating illiteracy. That mortgage will be removed fairly soon and we will have not only a House of Commons mortgage-free, but also a society that is fully equipped to move into the 21st century and compete not only in North America but all around the world. We could move Canada from where we are right now into the leading edge.

short-sighted when we on the one hand are doing this and on the other hand are producing reports that say we are not competitive because we are not educating people properly, particularly when we are dealing with countries like Japan and Germany. Not to be lost in the seriousness of what the hon. member for Ottawa Centre brings out, I just want to bring to the attention of the House that there are 14 or 15 payments that are going to be cut out of provinces. It is horrible to read a report called Funding Health and Higher Education, Danger Looming. I have part of this report here. If we follow the trend that is now taking place, it will reach $16 billion by the end of the century. The cumulative loss to the provinces at that time will be almost $100 billion.
Let me tell you what the report says. The figures are startling. I see the minister of health will be listening to this as well.
They project that the federal cash payments to Quebec will be gone by 1996. That is only a few years from now. Cash payments to Ontario will end by fiscal year 2002. The last federal cash payment to any province or territory, having stopped with Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and all the other provinces, will take place to the Yukon territories in fiscal year 2008 and 2009.
I think that is unacceptable. I see a lot of members on both sides of the House shaking their heads. They cannot believe it. People who are watching these presentations go back to when this budget was introduced in February and are saying: "Is this coming back to haunt us?" This is the bill that will make that budget law. I think many of us, if not most of us on this side of the House are going

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-20 is not the first time that this government has participated in further cutbacks to the provinces for health and post-secondary funding, but in dealing with this bill we see clearly the philosophical gap between this government and most Canadians. We see a gap which most Canadians would urge the government to close. We see a situation that indicates that the
government is clearly not in step with the wishes, desires and aspirations of other Canadians.
In Canada we have something which separates us from many other countries. It particularly separates us from the United States. We have joint federal and provincial fundings and commitments to health care, to post-secondary education, to our social safety net, and to our unemployment insurance program among others.
In other words we have a sort of social contract across Canada. Canadians expect and anticipate that their governments, provincial or federal, will participate in health care, will participate in post-secondary education and will participate in the social safety net. They will not only participate in those programs, but they will work to enhance them and improve them, not work to undermine them.
What we have seen across this country are provincial Liberal and Conservative governments that have undermined those programs, that have cut funding to health care, education and social assistance. We have seen a federal government which has consistently since 1984 undermined those very programs which are so important to most Canadians.
These programs, the federal and provincial support programs for health care, post-secondary education and for our social safety net, are important to Canadians because they make important statements about what sort of country Canada is and about who we are as Canadians.
They say that Canada as a country cares about its citizens when times are tough. It cares about its citizens when they are sick. It encourages and helps its citizens to obtain the highest level of education possible so that they can go on to make a valuable contribution to society.
The programs that Bill C-20 undermines are programs which are very important to Canadians.
In addition to cutting funding to the provinces for health care and education, this bill also increases the costs to employees and employers of the unemployment insurance fund, a fund which is designed to protect Canadians when they lose their jobs through no fault of their own and need some assistance in order to survive through the period before they get their next job, hopefully. It would provide them with the assistance to feed their families and keep their homes together.
December 3, 1991

The undermining of the commitment by the federal government to the unemployment insurance fund, cutting back on its funding, making it more difficult for Canadians to obtain unemployment insurance and forcing Canadians to have that protection for a shorter period of time, all those things are as a result of reductions in the federal government's commitment to unemployment insurance and have hurt ordinary Canadians severely.
When Bill C-20 was in committee, all the witnesses who came before the committee told the committee that this was a bill that would hurt ordinary Canadians. It would hurt our health care system. It would hurt our post-secondary education system and it would hurt Canadians who would be in need of unemployment insurance from time to time. Every group pointed out that this could be another nail in the coffin of medicare in this country. The freezing of contributions to the provinces for yet more years, the underfunding which has already taken place, the deterioration of our health care system which is already clear across the country to anyone who wants to go and see it, and the longer line-ups for surgery for health care, all these things will be made worse as a result of Bill C-20. All the witnesses who came before the committee advised the committee of that.

In government, the Official Opposition, the Liberal Party, began this process which the new government took on itself with a great deal of vigour. The time has come to invest in the future, to invest in Canada, to invest in Canadians. There are other approaches than this ratcheting down of the economy that this government is pursuing. There are other approaches than cutting back on social services, cutting back on health care, at a time when people need them most, cutting back on post-secondary education when that is the one way that we will be able to get out of our economic difficulties.

either the Japanese example or at a country like Austria, which has followed a full employment policy, which has ensured very low levels of unemployment, which has controlled inflation, which has controlled its currency value to a desirable level, which has dealt with foreign ownership in an effective way, which has addressed the investment problems and research problems and so on of its economy, a country like that took the creation of unemployment as its main goal in economic policy and it built everything else around that.
There was not an ignoring of inflation, an ignoring of the currency, and so on, ignoring of other economic indicators. There was a clear recognition that the way to fix the economy was to make sure that people were working, to follow a full employment policy. Neither the Liberal federal government nor the Conservative government has ever pursued a full employment policy and neither have the provinces. None of them have put unemployment as the first order of business.
We see inflation as a problem. What do we see Liberal and Conservative governments doing across the country? They create unemployment to reduce inflation. Ordinary Canadians pay the price for government policies which have not worked.
The way to deal with all of these issues in those countries which have followed full employment policies is, of course, to deal with these matters in a co-operative way with business, government and labour sitting down together to deal with the critical economic issues of the day. That works in Scandinavian countries and, as I say, in Austria. It provides people with security, it provides people with jobs and it provides people with a participation in the decision-making process.
The last point I want to make is that if we have those full employment policies, if we have Canadians working, they can provide for their families. They can buy the food they need. They can provide the housing they need. They do not need to have them provided by a social safety net.
They will of course at times need the social safety net. They might be unemployed at different times in their lives and they will need the security, the cushion of an unemployment insurance program. By working, they will
