Mr. Speaker, I want to say again, as I do on every occasion, how privileged I am to rise in this House on debate, specifically on this important Bill C-20.
Bill C-20 has rung many alarm bells across this country because of its implications for that most venerable of our social policies, medicare. It also has implications of course for post-secondary education and it is tied into the effort the Conservative government has been trying to make toward eradicating illiteracy.
These two areas of responsibility are of course under provincial jurisdiction, but the federal government is able to direct the policies because it pays the bills. We pay the bills. The legislation before us moves the federal government away from its monetary commitments in these areas. The implications for the continuation of these programs remains grim to say the least under this government.
We have to ask ourselves: If there is less money coming from the federal government to the provinces to support these programs of which I speak, is the federal government still able to direct national standards? The message from Canadians, from my constituents in Hamilton West, I believe is that they do not want the

Government Orders
federal government to abandon its traditional role in supporting these programs and enforcing national standards. The government must continue to support in fiscal and policy areas full national standards.
The main purpose of this bill is to put into effect the provision to extend the freeze on Established Programs Financing or transfers, as we like to call them, to the provinces until the year 1995. It is the former Minister of Finance's legacy to this country.
It is medicare that would be most effective under this scheme because of the way it is treated under the governing statute of medicare, the Canada Health Act.
My concern and that of my constituents to whom I have spoken as recently as today is the impact this bill, Bill C-20, will have on our treasured and highly respected social and health and education programs. Bill C-20 is the government's big-stick approach, a deliberate attack on, among other things, the very future of the medicare system in our country.
Canadians are proud of their social systems, especially medicare. We are familiar with the difference between our health care system and the health care system we witness in the United States. People need to have huge amounts of insurance coverage because health care as we all know is so very expensive there. In Canada we take it for granted.
I do not mean that in a negative way. What I mean is that there is a medicare system there for us to rely on wherever and whenever we need it. Of course this makes it universal in scope.
It is that veiy universality that is under attack in this particular piece of legislation, Bill C-20. Health care is a provincial responsibility, but the federal government calls the shots on how it is to be organized because it has the money. The less money that the federal government has at its disposal to expend, the less clout it is going to have enforcing provisions of the Canada Health Care Act.
Let us imagine for just a moment the worst case scenario in a breakdown of this system we are speaking about. This would be where in one less affluent province health care resources would be extremely strained. In another more affluent province, health care would have greater resources. What is the end result? It would create a system that would no longer be universal from
coast to coast to coast, but a patchwork quilt where good health care depended upon what part of the country you lived in.
The concerns that are coming out of my constituency are very real. The health care act, our public medicare system of course is one of the cornerstones, one of the building blocks of this great nation. As I mentioned earlier, I had a chance to speak with some of the hospital administrators in my riding.
In Hamilton we are proud, we boast, that we have the Hamilton Civic Hospitals, that is Henderson Hospital and the General. We boast that we have St. Joseph's Hospital in the downtown core. We have, of course, the Chedoke McMaster Hospital. Many a member in this Chamber I am sure is familiar with the McMaster University Medical Centre.
What are they are saying? If you want a direct quote from one of them I will give it to you. "Because of the financial situation we are in this year, we are survivable". Survivable. "Next year it is going to be a bitch".
Why? Probably because they foresee in their budgets a deficit that will be created next year and probably stay with us for three years, they say. A deficit of $5 million to $9 million is the possible in 1992. That is on a budget of just over $220 million.
What do they need at these hospitals in Hamilton to sustain the services and the programs they have initiated for next year? They say they need between 6 per cent and 7 per cent. That would maintain the current services and programs where they are today.
Because of cutbacks in transfer payments, reassessments, et cetera, they are guessing that they are going to get an increase, not of 6 and 7 per cent, but of only 2 per cent. What is that going to result in? The answer is obvious. It is going to impact on our programs and our services. It will mean cutbacks.
We heard from other members from the Toronto area where those cutbacks are going to happen. They have already begun. Wards have closed. People are being laid off.
What about Hamilton? In the great city of Hamilton we have cancer research programs, cardiovascular and neuroscience programs. We have the burns unit and the trauma program which are second to none in the world.

What are they facing next year? Deficits. What are they facing? Two per cent increases.
This government is tampering dangerously with a medicare system that is second to none. If anything else, it is feeling the insecurity. These hospitals in the Hamilton area, in Burlington, in Halton-Peel and in other areas across this country are feeling the insecurity of the pending budget crisis they may face by the end of their fiscal year, March 31 of next year. They are on pins and needles.
They ask themselves if there are going to be savings. The government hopes that with this bill and other parts of its strategy to save X amount of money.
The hospital administrators tell me the government is going to try to save X amount of money and in order to save that money at that particular hospital, it will have to close a service. Do Canadians want that kind of a system? I say no. This bill does not create that kind of gap, but I believe this bill and the continued administration of medicare under this government put the system on a slippery slope toward an uncertain future for medicare in this country.

The irony is that the government is crying poor. It never mentions that $4 million per hour every hour of the day, every day of the year, leaves Canada for the United States in investment income payments-$4 million per hour. That is roughly, at an estimate, $34 billion per year. This has been accelerating because of the government's policy in making it easy for the United States to take over more and more Canadian industries, either diverting the profits to the United States or diverting the the best paid jobs to the United States, or sometimes simply closing the operation, as they did with Inglis washing machine in Trinity Spadina and throwing 700 or 800 people out on the street in order to sell from the United States what used to be produced by Canadian workers.
By ciying poor, after giving all that money to rich Canadians and allowing more and more of the wealth of Canada to flow out to the United States at the rate of

December 3, 1991
Government Orders
many billions of dollars per year, the government now wants to chop about $4.5 billion out of the programs that serve the basic needs of Canadian people. It wants to limit, through this bill, the annual increase of provinces through the major transfer programs to $1 billion per year until 1995. At the same time it has half a billion dollars more for war, though we have never been in such a peace situation as we are now, it gives $30 million more for secret police, the CSIS, without of course any opportunity for Canadians to find out what is being done with that budget because it is secret, and therefore less for health, less for education, less for social assistance and, as I said, zero from the government for unemployment insurance, except a law that will increase the fees at a time when workers have less to pay with.
I want to speak for a few minutes about our health system. Previous speakers have referred to it. I think it bears not only emphasizing the points they made, but adding to them. In Canada we developed a national health care system that had five important principles. One was comprehensive. It does not cover every imaginable health cost, but it covers nearly all of them, prevents people going into bankruptcy with health problems and enables people to have their health care paid for when they are flat on their back in bed and unable to earn the money, which is the most important of all.
It is universal. Everybody is entitled. The poor are not left out because they are poor.
It is portable. You talk about unity in our country, unity between the provinces. When the government cuts back its central share of the funding for the health programs, provinces will be under pressure to say, as occasionally they say now, but only occasionally: "No, you cannot come into our hospital because you live in another province. You may be a Canadian but you cannot come into our province for health care because we do not want to pay for the health care needs of somebody from another province". The whole principle of portability was meant to ensure that a Canadian could get the health care he or she needs anywhere in Canada regardless of provincial jurisdiction. It should be accessible, and there has been a good expansion of health care systems into even the outlying parts of our country. It has not gone as far as it is needed but it is going that way, and it is administered publicly. Therefore, it was efficient by comparison with the chaotic, that is to say market system
of health in our neighbour to the south. I will be coming back to that later.
The federal government has the responsibility for ensuring these five principles by the original deal of 50/50 funding, matching the provinces dollar for dollar. That was eroded under the Liberals and it is being downgraded further and will eventually disappear or become quite insignificant under the present Tory government.
This is a program that began in Saskatchewan under the CCF and the New Democratic Party and was so evidently a good program that other provinces insisted on having it and the federal government, in the sixties particularly, established it. It is if not the best in the world, certainly one of the very best, and it is recognized that way especially by our neighbour to the south, or at least by the people of our neighbour to the south, not necessarily by the government.
The NDP believes that we must direct more resources toward health rather than less in order to keep pace with the new health threats in our country, such as the threats from environmental degradation. There is a health need now to provide preventive health care and remedying of the poisonous elements that we put into our environment, which would in the long run save a good deal of money in acute health care.
I want to make several points about the Canadian health system. In the United States, they spend about $600 billion a year on health care, but 40 million Americans have no health insurance protection whatsoever. The United States is the only country in the world, other than South Africa, without some form of public health care system.
Second, universal availability is the basis of a system that gives priority to efficiency over competition. The chaotic market competitive system to the south of us spends far more money per person on health care than Canada does and it gets poorer results, less health, less lives saved for more money because they do not have a universal availability and a public administration. For example, in the United States they spend about $2,268 per capita for their health coverage, while Canadians spend $1,580, less than two-thirds of what they spend in the United States. It costs $360 per day on average to
December 3, 1991

stay in an American hospital compared to $210 in Canada-that is $360 Canadian.
Further, most western countries have stabilized their medicare budgets, but not the United States-the United States, the land where the market reigns, where if you cannot pay you can be turned away from the hospital no matter how sick and needy you are. In 1987 the U.S. health care costs rose to more than 11 per cent of the Gross National Product, compared to 8.5 per cent of the Gross National Product in Canada. In some European countries they are even lower with roughly the same sort of health care system that Canada has, and they spend an average of 7.5 per cent of their Gross National Product.
The Canadian system is more efficient. Canadians are hospitalized for 11.4 days on average and the Americans for 6.4 days because of the more intensive use of technology. Utilization rates are higher in Canada. In 1989, 37.2 per cent of American doctors were sued for accusations of malpractice. That means that some of them are avoiding certain medical procedures because they are too risky. In other words, our system is working better.
The rate of production of physicians in Canada and the United States has been about equal, but the main difference between Canada and the States is that in the United States, physician fees have been rising far faster than the inflation rate.
In Canada they were dropping in the 1970s. They have now risen slightly but they are still a little bit behind the inflation rate.
The result is that in Canada the average life expectancy at birth is 72.9 years for men, 79.8 years for women, whereas in the United States it is only 71 years for men and 78.3 years for women. So men and women in Canada live longer than in the United States because of our health system.
Canada's infant mortality rate in 1985 was 7.9 deaths per 100,000 live births. In the United States it was 25 per cent more at 10.6 deaths per 100,000. The United States is down at twentieth on the international list for infant mortality. Canada is fifth to the lowest.
Canadians are allowed greater freedom of choice of their doctors. I hear from my son who is presently living
Government Orders
in San Francisco that there is a debate going on in the media there about the Canadian health system. People say that there is a problem with it. Then somebody writes a letter to the paper saying that there is not and they were there. One person claimed that you could not choose your doctor and another person who was from Canada said you can choose your doctor.
In New York they have a state legislature bill. The New York members of the National Congress have a bill in Congress as well to bring in a health care system modelled on the Canadian one. The American labour movement is pushing strongly to establish a health care system modelled on the Canadian one. In fact, they have invited members of the NDP to go to the United States to tell them about the health system. Yet in this country, the government wants to undermine it and push it into privatization,.
Canadians are fairly well satisfied with their health care system and one of the reasons for the satisfaction is that a doctor has little financial reason to refuse a patient. This happens too often in the United States when a person goes to a hospital or a doctor, is asked to pay in advance and may not be able to and is turned away.
It is disastrous for this government to undermine our health system with the kind of cuts it is making with Bill C-20. It is also disastrous to be cutting the money for post-secondary education. Students are dropping out of their studies for financial reasons. Sometimes it is simply too much to be working at a job and studying as well. They cannot stop eating, so they have to stop studying. Some students are coming out with intolerable debts that they cannot pay while they are unemployed for a year, two and three years or when they are under-employed.
The universities are in effect becoming mortgaged to private industry for funds. That is to say, they have to do the research that private industry thinks will benefit this or that particular segment of industry, instead of doing the basic research that would make our country much stronger, not only technically, but intellectually in the broader sense and worldly, instead of giving a broad education.
It is ironic. There are few other white headed people in this House of Commons who can remember 1945 when we came out of the armed forces and were offered the veterans affairs programs. The Department of Veter-

Government Orders
ans Affairs said it would help us set up a business, build a home, get into farming or go to university. I got $60 a month and tuition paid. With a very small amount of work, usually in the summertime, I was able to manage on that. It was raised later to $80 and, two or three years later, to $100. They gave us a monthly allowance as long as we were studying and our grades on the exams passed a reasonable level. The attitude surely was that study is work and useful to Canada. Canada paid us to study.
Tens of thousands of Canadians went to university on DVA who would never have gone otherwise. I was not one of those because I was fortunate enough that because of my parents' circumstances, I would have gone anyway. Some of those people became brilliant in science, industry and finance. Some of them are still members of this House. And yet the government wants to cut off that possibility in Canada.
There is also the matter of public assistance in which Canada has a worse record than Britain or West Germany. We have 14 per cent of people in poverty and are cutting back on public assistance. Germany has only 7 per cent, Britain has 9 per cent and Norway and Sweden have 5 per cent living in poverty. And of course, there is the UI cutback.
What we have is not an attempt to balance a budget or pay a deficit, because the deficit was created by gifts to the rich. It is a class attack. It is an attack by the class of owners of industries, by the corporations and their major shareholders, on the people who must earn their living by working. It cuts their pay and humiliates them. It is building up massive anger and a massive demand for a change in the power system in Canada.
I wish this government would ease off because the change may be more chaotic and even more violent, considering what we see in the newspapers, than any of us could wish. We should be negotiating between the government and the people of Canada for a decent opportunity to work, a decent opportunity to live and a sense that people belong to each other rather than just competitive dog-eat-dog philosophy in the service of American-based corporations.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Funk (Prince Albert-Churchill River) moved:
speechtext:
That this House calls on the government to support the foundation of consumer-run Community Health Centres, which have preventive health care as a principle of operation, and which engage medical professionals to provide services in salaried or contractual positions, as opposed to the traditional billing arrangements.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am privileged to be able to put this motion before the House today because it is something that I consider to be a very important subject.
Private Members' Business
It is somewhat ironic that we are discussing this private member's motion on the very same day that we have heard a number of speeches in this House with respect to Bills C-20 and C-69, which deal with the cutbacks that have been happening in the medicare system and the threat which our medicare system is being put under as a result of these cuts.
It is ironic to me that we are spending all this time discussing the negative aspects of what is happening to our national health care system while at the same time we devote so little time talking about positive alternatives. In that respect I guess I am sorry that this is not a votable motion because I think this would offer members an opportunity to say something positive about health care rather than continuing this endless round of cuts and more cuts.
I think Canadians are acutely aware of the funding crisis in the medicare system. At the same time they still hold the medicare system intensely dear.
They are very much committed to the basic notions of medicare. Medicare has become a fundamental part of the fabric of this country.
The Spicer commission reported that across this country, in every province and in every community, medicare is seen as the primary vehicle or the primary institution that holds this country together.
It is perhaps interesting to note that in the constitutional debate people are finding it somewhat difficult to put a handle on the notion of what a social charter might mean and also what the political implications of a referendum might be. I would suggest that if we put to Canadians the notion that medicare should be entrenched in the Constitution of Canada, we would have virtually unanimous support for that idea from coast to coast.
I think we have seen other evidence that health care is still a resonant issue not only in Canada but in North America. The election of Senator Wofford in the recent Pennsylvania senatorial race is a good example. That senator ran on the slogan of "why should criminals be entitled to a lawyer when you are not entitled to a doctor?"
That sounded a real chord with the people of Pennsylvania and with the American public. They are debating medicare actively, and Canadians are looking for an active and positive debate on the future of medicare as well.

Private Members' Business
I would also, at the beginning of this speech, like to mention that much of my interest in the subject of community health centres comes from my own community of Prince Albert. The people of Prince Albert, when confronted with the crisis of the doctors' strike in 1962, did something about it. They organized a community health centre around the work of a physician by the name of Orville Hjertaas.
It was one of the most dramatic moments in the history of medicare in this country and I think it deserves special attention in the annals of medicare.
In Prince Albert we have demonstrated all the things that I am going to speak about later in the speech. The community health model is cheaper, it is more cost effective, it is better at doing preventive care and it involves people in the community.
Community health centres start from a fundamentally different premise than our regular model of health care. That is because they are based in community experience, and are organized and founded within the community by local people. From development on, they are inherently community based.
They are all run by volunteer boards elected by the community, whether they are organized on a co-operative basis or on some other type of non-profit organization basis.
There have been lots of studies done about the community health centres in this country. I want to mention that there are some very successful models in this country, apart from the one in Prince Albert.
There are community clinics in Winnipeg, in Montreal, in Vancouver, in rural Prince Edward Island and in northern Ontario. All of these provide very positive models not only in their own communities, but to us nationally.
For example, in a paper by Douglas Angus and Pran Manga sponsored by the Canadian Co-operative Association and with help from the co-op secretariat of the federal government entitled Co-op Consumer Sponsored Health Care Delivery Effectiveness, they concluded that the community health centres are efficient and effective.
A 1982 government of Saskatchewan study compared 15,297 community clinic users and 15,297 private practice patients matched for all socioeconomic variables.
It is interesting to note that the former government of Saskatchewan refused to release this report which was commissioned in 1982 and completed in about 1984 or 1985. It did not release it until 1989 because I think it did not like the implications of it, which say that we need a wholesale change in the way we look at health care.
The findings of these studies were that over-all health service costs were 13 per cent to 17 per cent lower for community clinic patients than for private practice patients, 13 per cent to 17 per cent lower.
I would like to quote from the authors: "The principle reason for cost effectiveness is the significantly lower hospital utilization by clinic clientele compared to those of fee for service practitioners". They continue to say that this lower utilization of hospital facilities is the most significant and incontrovertible finding of numerous empirical studies they have reviewed.
Non-fee for service systems generate rates of hospital utilization from 10 to 40 per cent below fee for service physicians.
These findings are corroborated by those in larger population studies in U.S. community clinics.
Twenty per cent savings in hospital costs and patient days lead to a saving in over-all costs of about 5 per cent to 8 per cent in just this one aspect alone, hospitalization. That is the fastest growing component in health care costs.
The clinics have also been found to have a better record in providing childhood immunizations, cancer screening, cancer prevention services, preventive health maintenance for women, for seniors, for expectant mothers. All of these things mean healthier patients, lower drug costs, and lower costs to the community in general.
MDs and community clinics prescribe fewer prescription drugs which have cost and health advantages. Provision of out-patient services and support services
December 3, 1991

like X-rays, labs, and physiotherapy can cost substantially less than the same services in hospitals.
Preventive measures like well-baby clinics, geriatric dietary care and awareness education about violence against women and children can all be incorporated in the community health model which then makes not only for lower costs but for a much healthier population and a much healthier community.
I might also add that we are living in a day and age when people are demanding more say in their over-all lives. They are demanding that they have some control over the institutions that give them services and surely community health services give people an opportunity to get directly involved in providing their own health care. We also have seen that health care is something that people are individually very interested about in this country and it is something they would get involved in.
Another advantage of clinics is to respond to the wide diversity of needs in this country. There are clinics specializing in services to new Canadians, to urban aboriginal Canadians, to rural aboriginal Canadians and to farm communities. The variety is infinite when it comes to the types of models which can be adapted to reflect particular local circumstances.
Community health centres are also cost effective because they are administered by professional health administrators. Very few private practices have that kind of management training.
As well, budgeting and cost control for primary health care are easier for provincial governments to control because budgets are negotiated on a global basis which makes them predictable from year to year and makes it possible to do the kind of evaluations which show whether money is being well spent.
I think what rings the loudest in the context of the debate here in Parliament today is the cost saving of 13 per cent to 17 per cent. Let us put that in some kind of a context. In 1990 total health care expenditures in Canada are estimated to be $60 billion. That is 9 per cent of our Gross National Product or $2,266 per person. These costs are rising at about 12 per cent per year. We know that.
Imagine that with this basic change to how we view the delivery of health here, we could save from 13 per cent to 17 per cent of the $60 billion cost. Even at 10 per cent
Private Members' Business
we are talking about $6 billion worth of savings and that is not something that this country can ignore in its present fiscal situation. The federal government cannot ignore that kind of possible saving, nor can provincial governments.
What is the federal government's role in this? I think that is a legitimate question to ask because the federal government seems to be seeking a smaller and smaller role in the whole health care area. In keeping with its cutback in funding it also seems to be withdrawing from what it formerly saw as a leadership role in the delivery of health care to Canadians and especially the establishment of medicare.
Certainly those two aspects, the establishment of medicare and the establishment of national standards, remain federal government responsibilities.
The government has also talked in the past about more active participation in health care. Certainly this government has. In November 1966 the Hon. Jake Epp, the then minister of health, now the minister of energy, released a blueprint for direction of health care delivery in Canada entitled Achieving Health for All: A Framework for Health Promotion. It outlined a system of health care wholly consistent with that promoted by the co-operative and community based health centre concept.
There are three strategies outlined in that report.
It called for the encouragement of greater public participation; the strengthening of community services and the co-ordination of public policy. All three of those fit exactly into the framework of community health centres and co-operative clinics. What kind of action have we had from of the government?
When researching this speech I saw a pretty dismal picture. In the Department of National Health and Welfare there is exactly one person working full time on community based, consumer oriented health care-one person working on clinics in community based health care. That is in a year in which the Department of National Health and Welfare is listed as having a total of
8.500	people working in it. Having one person out of
8.500	working on this delivery system, which could save us 13 per cent to 17 per cent of our health care costs, is just plain stupid.
We have seen this kind of lip-service from the government, but we have not seen much action. We have also seen supporting evidence from the provincial level. The

December 3, 1991
Private Members' Business
Seaton report, recently released in B.C., strongly endorses the community health care model. In Ontario, a discussion paper called New Beginnings, released by the Ontario Ministry of Health, concluded that community sponsored organizations were better at achieving objectives of broad-based service provisions and cost containment than non-community sponsored forms of care. In Saskatchewan the new government campaigned with preventive community based care as one of its central campaign planks.
Provincial governments across the country are reaching the same conclusion: this is the direction to go in. Somebody has to take some leadership in this. With the cutbacks coming from the federal government, certainly the latitude that it has to be spending money in this area is drastically curtailed. The leadership that was promised from the federal level, first in the Jake Epp report and then later by the ministers of co-operation, is simply not there.
A few years ago we had a federal-provincial co-operatives ministers meeting, I believe in the spring of 1989, which identified as one of its four principal priorities the encouragement and establishment of community health based models across this country-a co-operative health based model. That was identified as one of the four major priorities with the full endorsement of the federal government. There were all kinds of speeches made and press releases about the leadership government was going to take. Where is that leadership? It is not there.
There are other areas in which the government could get involved in promoting the community health concept. There is a lot of work done in the areas of poverty, nutrition and health. These areas could best be addressed through the community clinics. Family violence initiatives could be delivered through community clinics. Community health could become a part of housing initiatives.
Certainly the whole area of native health lends itself very well to the integration of a community health system because it offers a primary way in which the traditional healing methods and the community support structures which are inherent in the native community could be melded with the scientific health model in a way which is appropriate to those communities. We do not see that kind of initiative from the federal government, although it has a clear mandate in the area of native health.
The federal government also has to resolve jurisdictional disputes in many areas. We also have the questions of women's health needs, and support to women and children in crisis, which are also areas in which community clinics can offer a primary support mechanism. We have the unmet health needs of Canada's poor. We have drug abuse problems in many of our communities.
The government could play a key role in being a catalyst in all these areas. It could put together a national co-ordination strategy involving the provinces, involving the co-operative sector, involving existing community health models in establishing this new framework for a Canadian health strategy. Certainly there is a lot of activity under way. In Ontario the government is going full speed ahead with the best resources it has available. Forty-one clinics are already in existence, another 25 to 30 are in process.
These community health centres need money for feasibility studies and planning. They need help to get organized, they need help for a national organization. We are not talking about big sums of money, we are talking about very minute sums of money, seed money, which would result in a saving of 13 per cent to 17 per cent in the system over-all.
I would like to conclude my speech by saying that I think a case has been very well made by many people that community sponsored health centres, health centres where the professionals who are working there are there on salaries and not on a fee for service basis, offer not only the most cost effective but the most community sensitive and the most efficient in terms of preventive health models of any model of health care in the country.
I might say there is another reason why I would like to address this question, because many of us are wondering if our health system is so wonderful and if the Americans are wanting to copy it, how come our health system is in so much trouble? There is a good reason for that. It is because only half of medicare has ever been implemented.
I remember very well in 1962 when medicare was introduced in Saskatchewan. My family was one of only two or three families in our community that supported the establishment of medicare, and it was a very bitter time in those communities. I remember being harassed in the school yard along with the children of other people who supported the establishment of medicare,
December 3, 1991

and many other people in Saskatchewan had similar experiences.
The doctors went on strike, backed by not only the Canadian Medical Association but the American Medical Association. The Conservative Party and the Liberal Party of the day backed the doctors in that strike. It was a tremendous struggle. Therefore the system that Tommy Douglas introduced was based on insuring existing health care. But Tommy Douglas said at the time: "This is only the first step. This step is certainly needed in order that everybody have access to health care, a universal system but a second step is needed". A second step is needed to provide medical care on a cost effective community based system that actually meets the needs of everyone. Tommy Douglas was right from the start about the need to establish a co-operative and community health centre based system of medicare. If we are going to be true to the founders of medicare, if we are going to bail ourselves out of the crisis we are in, this is the route to go.
I would like to urge all members of this House and particularly the members on the government side to take this motion very seriously and to act on it because I think in many ways the future of our country and what it stands for is at stake.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the hon. member for Prince Albert-Churchill River knows that the delivery and organization of health services is under provincial jurisdiction.
In spite of that, our government is keenly concerned about the efficient and effective delivery of health services and, together with the provinces, it is exploring new ways to provide for the greater welfare of all Canadians.
We are aware that many provincial studies in the last five or six years show the need to rethink the way services are provided and health professionals are paid for their medical services.
The recently published report of the British Columbia Royal Commission of Inquiry on Health shows as well as anything the serious thinking now going on throughout
Private Members' Business
the country on this subject. The authors recognize that moving from a simple health care system to a health promotion system requires us to explore many different avenues. An approach cannot be considered without taking into account possible repercussions on other areas for any change made to the system.
The British Columbia report contains over 400 recommendations, which shows how complex this issue is. Therefore it would be utopian to claim that one particular approach would solve all the problems of our health care system. That would be too simple. It would also dismiss the considerable efforts made by health professionals and Canadian health care institutions to improve Canadians' health from coast to coast.
It is true that our health systems tended to favour an approach to health based on institutional services and to use payment methods that emphasized treatment itself instead of an integrated approach. After reflection, the provinces moved toward a more balanced system that takes into account a wide range of possible approaches for dealing with various situations. Health centres could be one of those avenues and they could be patterned on the model suggested by the hon. member.
We must not forget that these issues are in provincial jurisdiction, but the government can, and does, help the provinces compile the information needed to consider them in greater depth. The federal-provincial-territorial conference of deputy ministers of health endorsed the recent Barer-Stoddart report on integrated policies for medical staff in Canada. The authors of that report make a number of recommendations concerning the remuneration of doctors. At their meeting in September 1991, the provincial and territorial health ministers agreed that in future discussions based on this report could be undertaken with all interested parties.
The government also helps the provinces to develop their own policy using the national data base on doctors which provides information on payments made to doctors under the fee for service system. Attempts are being made to expand this data base to include other forms of payment. It is impossible to make good decisions without this type of data and thanks to the partnership between the government and the provinces, a picture of the payment situation across the country will emerge.

December 3, 1991
Private Members' Business
I am pleased to see that the hon. member displays such interest in users' involvement in health issues. I believe that he takes "user" to mean anyone who benefits from the health care system in Canada. The government encourages Canadians to take part in improving their own health. In 1986, the Minister of National Health and Welfare published a report entitled: Achieving Health for All: A Framework for Health promotion. The authors of that document proposed three key strategies to reduce inequalities and increase prevention. They especially emphasized the importance of promoting public participation and strengthening community health services.
All federal prevention campaigns, such as the national drug strategy, the national AIDS strategy and the national tobacco strategy emphasize user participation. People want to participate and they bring all their knowledge and experience to bear in supporting these programs in their communities.
Active public participation is beneficial in more than one way. When people care about community problems and work together to solve them, three things happen: first, they become more aware of the various parts of the problem and they learn more about prevention; second, they help raise their community's awareness and they become real agents of change; third, the services and programs developed with the community are usually more responsive to local needs and more effective because they have public support.
The federal government's funding programs directly support public participation in all health-related issues. The Department of National Health and Welfare financially supports more than 70 voluntary national health and social service organizations. Some particular programs also receive financial assistance through various programs like New Horizons, the Seniors Independence Program, the Family Violence Initiative and the Health Promotion Fund. The government is proud to act as a partner and to contribute to the success of projects set up across the country in all communities, large and small. This partnership is very beneficial and helps achieve results that we could not achieve alone.
Some of these results are tangible, others less so. I already said that by working together, we can increase public awareness and make programs more effective. But those who are active in their community gain considerable benefits: they acquire more self-confidence and are better able to make enlightened decisions about their own health and the health of those close to them. Some will say that we gave them the power and the required resources. I think that they simply realized their own strength.
This partnership is also good financially. For every dollar that the government gives national volunteer organizations in the health field, they obtain $80 million which they spend on education, prevention and research.
It is definitely in our interest to encourage the health care recipients to participate. However, this participation will only be beneficial if they have the required skills and resources to examine problem areas or potential solutions, to come up with valid approaches and work out the many details that are often overlooked but nevertheless essential to the success of a project.
The government intends to give users easier access to the planning tools they need to set up good programs. For this purpose, the department has created a community action information kit. It contains usual information as well as tools to promote setting up community action programs. This kit was put together in consultation with the provinces as well as many community groups and organizations across the country.
This goes to show, the government's concern for the problem raised by the hon. member for Prince Albert- Churchill River and that we work closely with the provinces in dealing with this issue. The creation of consumer-run community health centers is strictly a matter of provincial jurisdiction. However, our government intends to continue supporting the efforts of the provinces that are trying to identify areas of priority thus making for a fairer system better suited to promote health in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to rise to speak on this private members' motion put forward by my colleague from Prince Albert-Churchill River.
The motion reads:
That this House calls on the government to support the foundation of consumer run Community Health Centres, which have preventive health care as a principle of operation, and which engage medical professionals to provide services in salaried or contractual positions, as opposed to the traditional billing arrangements.
I am pleased to speak to this motion. I believe the operation of health centres in the Western Arctic may be a model for consumer run health centres. I will give more detail on our system later.
It is appropriate that we are dealing with this motion on the day that the Etouse is debating Bill C-20, a bill that should clearly be scrapped and replaced by a commitment from government to support our vital and universal health care system.
I want to say at the outset that a universal medicare program is essential to Liberal policy and philosophy and basically to Canadian philosophy. The Liberal Party is opposed to the abuse of the medicare system and to extra billing. I do not want to take the time to debate the accepted principles of medicare, those of universality, accessibility, portability, comprehensiveness and public administration. Instead, I will focus on delivery of health services and the supply responsibilities and enumeration of health care professionals.
I support the idea that Canadians need to look at alternatives to ensure that health care services meet the needs of women, aboriginal people, the elderly and minorities. I support the concept that the federal government should complement the existing system of universal health care by permitting non-government facilities to provide much-needed services as long as those facilities use approved procedures, comply with government standards and charge rates that do not exceed amounts set by provincial-territorial health insurance plans.
Certainly the standing committee on health, which spent two years in developing its reports, made recommendations that received all-party support, intended to assist local control and more accessibility as well as a more diverse service than the traditional hospital and dispensary system. The first part of this motion deals
Private Members' Business
with consumer-run community house centres. I have to assume that the intent of the motion abides by the philosophy of non-profit and with the principles of the Canada Health Act.
In my riding we call this concept community-based health services. Community health centres traditionally called nursing stations and traditional hospitals are managed by regional health boards. In Western Arctic these regional health boards include one, the Mackenzie Health Services; two, the Fort Smith Health Board; three, Hay River H.W. Williams Memorial; four, Inuvik Health Board; and the fifth one is the Stanton Hospital Board in Yellowknife.
The theory that guides these boards is one of devolving control of health services to the community levels. These boards are representative of communities where they are responsible for health care centres. They also include some efforts by various departments in the government of the Northwest Territories that intervene in a positive way.
Just recently I was visiting Arctic College, in fact yesterday, in the town of Fort Smith where a group of students are now engaging in what is called an aboriginal medical terminology interpreter corps training which is very innovative and which would not have resulted without accessibility by people to the health care system. It is absolutely integral when you have a patient who is unilingual who cannot communicate their illnesses and their concerns to the medical professionals.
The local input and control of resources not only recognizes but acts on these very real concerns that individuals have at the local level. The government of the Northwest Territories took control over health programs from the federal government in 1988, so the establishment of these regional boards has taken place smoothly and successfully. There are always growing pains with such initiatives but it has been getting some fairly positive reviews in the Medical Post dated November 19, 1991. The headlines read that the Northwest Territories is glad to be in control of health care services since 1988.
There are comments that are made by people like the Inuvik Regional Nursing Officer, Sharon Conley, who feels that the Inuvik Health board for instance is working. "Since transfer", she says, "there has been a lot more local interest in health care. We can get things

done a lot quicker because we do not have decisions made in Ottawa through Yellowknife" she said.
These are the upsides of having local control over health services and having consumer-run health programs.
In the same article it states: "Officials of the Northwest Territories NWT Medical Association feel the transfers to the GNWT government has had positive results. It is stated that people who are in control are closer to the scene and they are more responsive to the needs of the territories. For instance the Inuvik Board consists of 17 members and consists of people from all the communities in the Inuvik region as well as governments and the aboriginal organizations".
It is a healthy, if I might, no pun intended, cross section of people to be sitting on a health board, a regional board that expresses the concerns and recognizes the concerns of the people who live in that particular area. The board's responsibilities include budgets, policies, the hiring of doctors and specialists. The boards ensure local involvement, particularly in the small and aboriginal communities.
The other area that is of particular concern is preventive health. This motion deals with preventive health care. The first cause of poor health in the north is inadequate substandard housing. The second cause is the environment within the house. This is a major reason why the northern territories lead the nation in illness and poor health.
As I stated in this House on November 29, the north experiences higher death and disease rates and higher birth and infant mortality rates than the rest of Canada. Cancer is four times greater and suicide is the highest in Canada. Many of the causes of these statistics are the poor housing situation and the general poor quality of life.
In the north we are starting with these basic requirements for infrastructure, for proper housing, water and sewage facilities. These are the things that are recognized by people that are in local control that feel the effects on their families and the people in our communities, people that they have to deal with on a daily basis, not just names and numbers that have no association to them. I am committed to preventive medicine. I believe
the government should strengthen its commitments to participation, to drug abuse prevention and AIDS education. I believe also that nursing stations and their personnel play a very key role along with the community health representatives who are trained. These facilities and the twinning with these other community health representatives are integral to the health and well-being of all citizens in the communities that do not have hospitals.
These nursing stations act as a centre of comfort for many who have to go there, where ambulances are not available, who rely on medical rescue missions in the middle of the night or in very inclement weather, under very adverse and harsh environmental realities. This is when the personnel who are situated in the communities are there with the approval, the consent and with the support of the regional health boards that put them there. They ensure we get the quality people we need. The training is very specific and is also very much one that is geared to the community. Most of the community health representatives speak the aboriginal languages of the communities they are in and they serve a very key role.
I want to commend my colleague, the member for Prince Albert-Churchill River, for coming forward with this very important private members' bill. I support it wholeheartedly. I believe that in the Northwest Territories we are a testimony to what can be done if we put control and resources into the hands of the people who understand their communities and can represent their people as well as anyone else in this country.
I believe that we have quality care and we have priorities set out that express what people need in terms of preventive medicine as well as other concerns that prevail over the territories.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for Prince Albert-Churchill River for giving us with this opportunity to discuss one of the most interesting areas of development for health systems in Canada. When dealing with health issues, we look at quality of life which concerns every Canadian man and woman.

December 3, 1991	COMMONS
Although the provision of health services is a provincial jurisdiction, the federal government has been looking into innovative ways to enhance the efficiency of our health systems for quite some time now. The work of Health and Welfare Canada is but an illustration of the government's commitment to support prevention and community oriented approaches to health. The department and its staff with training and experience in the areas of health, social services, community and volunteer work, education, research as well as program and policy development, supports programs that are useful to the operation of community health centres and works toward developing new programs in that area.
Our guiding principle in this endeavour is community participation because communities are capable of taking their health in their own hands and should take part in defining their needs and finding means of responding to these needs.
To help the growing number of community health centres across Canada, Health and Welfare Canada has published a health centre directory so that each centre knows what the others are doing in any given area. The department also produced an information package for community groups and workers. That package, which provides useful tools for action, has already been tested with community groups and health centres across the country. This is an excellent example of the co-operation shown by our government with the provinces and the volunteer groups to support their efforts to reinforce the role and the responsibility of individuals and the community in the field pf health and health services.
The notion of consumer involvement in the health sector is relatively new. Numerous possibilities must be explored, including the use of community development approaches.
The department sponsored research initiatives in that field through the National Health Research and Development Program. It has also financed, through a contribution program to health promotion, new community projects that use these approaches. Together we learn that the work undertaken has resulted in an exercise of co-operation between a number of provincial representatives, health centres, managers and of community health researchers.

Private Members' Business
These people made a concerted effort to determine how the community development approaches could be used efficiently in providing health services. This type of conceptual research and development can be very useful to define the role that community health centres managed by consumers can play in a balanced health care system.
We insist on the consumer participation in the hon. member's motion because we believe that the method used to set up health services is vital to their effectiveness. Many of the existing studies on the subject indicate that the most efficient methods are those based on an upward movement as well as community participation in the analysis of their health needs and the development of appropriate means to meet those needs.
Based on that community health development perspective, it seems that the community health centres managed by consumers have played a pioneer role. Indeed, we only have to look at one of the first initiatives, the local community service centres, commonly called CLSC in Quebec. As early as the beginning of the 1970s, the position of community organizer was created in the first few centres.
Another example are the community health centres in Ontario, where teams of workers were under the direction of community action co-ordinators and community development agents. These teams were mainly involved in prevention and community health promotion.
The hon. member for Prince Albert-Churchill River is certainly aware of the fact that community clinics of Saskatchewan set up as co-ops some 30 years ago were the first consumer-run health centres in Canada. As a matter of fact, these clinics were among the first to undergo exhaustive and serious studies which have revealed that a parallel system of community health centers saves a lot of money in health costs.
I am convinced that the hon. member is aware of the community health study the government of Saskatchewan carried out in 1983 which contains these findings. The Hastings report is another milestone document dealing with this issue. This report which was commissioned following a deputy ministers of health conference stressed the need for community health centres as tools

December 3, 1991
Private Members' Business
for managing health costs and supported the creation of many more such organizations.
Of course, this concept was not embraced everywhere overnight. If you look at provincial reports and studies published over the past few years, however, you can see that interest is growing. For instance, the New Brunswick Premier's Council on Health is in the process of evaluating how to apply the community health model in the province, while Quebec has reaffirmed its confidence in local community service centres.
Other provinces are examining the possibility of adopting similar models. Despite this growing interest throughout the country in consumer-run community health centres, we must admit that all provinces do not support this kind of centre in the same way.
Some provinces do not officially recognize these organizations as parallel models for health care delivery, while others have legislation in place and permanent funding mechanisms to give them a solid base.
In June 1991 representatives of co-operative or consumer-run community health centres from various regions met to consider the possibility of creating a national network. They felt that such a national organization would help guide discussion and facilitate information exchange.
The Canadian government will continue to follow with great interest the discussions on consumer-run community health centres. There are no miracle solutions to the problems facing our health care systems today. We believe that with good communication and serious consideration of the issues involved, Canadians will find an apt combination of approaches to meet their health care needs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are several aspects to this member's bill which we have been discussing here this evening which go beyond the responsibility of the federal government.
I think most of us know that health care delivery is primarily a provincial responsibility under the Constitution. The Canada Health Act, which came into force April 1, 1984, and embodies the basic principles that form the cornerstones of the Canadian health care system, only requires of a province that there be reasonable compensation to physicians and dentists for all insured health care services rendered.
December 3, 1991

It does not require specific organizational structures and/or particular modes of payment. I should point out that the Canada Health Act did pass this House with unanimous approval by all parties.
However, I would like you all to be aware that while the federal government does not want to tinker with the mechanism of provincial health care systems as perhaps the hon. member is suggesting, we do have an excellent record in providing support and encouragement to prevention in ways that do not interfere with the constitutional prerogatives of the provinces to manage their own health care systems.
The National Health Research and Development Program provides support for research projects, for studies, for demonstrations and evaluation projects and for the delivery of health care. There are other relevant categories of research, including health promotion and illness prevention, risk assessment, health of native peoples, rehabilitation and dissemination of health services research. These are all addressed by this national program.
I would now like to turn to the area of prevention, in which Canada is recognized as one of the world leaders. That is the integration of preventive services into primary care.
Interest in this topic was triggered well over a decade ago with the growing concern about the decreasing marginal benefits of the curative medical technologies in the context of the spiralling health care costs. In order to address this pressing problem in a truly rational manner and to help preserve the health care system of which Canadians are so justifiably proud, the conference of deputy ministers of health in 1976 established the Canadian task force on a periodic health examination. The task force was provided with a mandate to formulate recommendations that would help to integrate preventive activities into the practices of clinicians. The task force had to examine the appropriateness of a wide variety of preventive manoeuvres. This called for a massive review of the appropriate scientific literature that was out in the public domain, which was a very difficult task. If this was to have any meaning, it could not really be done in a haphazard manner.
Accordingly, the task force developed a rigorous evaluation process involving parameters such as the current burden of suffering related to the condition of being
Private Members' Business
prevented; as well as safety, simplicity, cost, and acceptability to the individual of course.
The group developed rules of evidence based upon rigorous criteria on how to rate the scientific literature support for preventive interventions. These rules of evidence led to a related classification of recommendations that advised physicians whether or not there was good, fair or poor evidence to do or not to do a preventive action.
As a result of their pioneering work in 1979, the Canadian task force on periodic health examination released a monograph addressing 78 selected conditions, accompanied by clinical practice recommendations that were tailored to patient age, gender and risk status.
In the field of clinical prevention, this was a report that was heard all around the world. Without any legislative base, the task force's recommendation was that annual check-ups for ostensibly healthy adults be abandoned and that primary care prevention be provided by lifetime programs based on age and sex-specific health protection packages.
This has had a major impact on the norms of preventive practice in several western countries. For example, in 1984 the United States Department of Health and Human Services established a preventive services task force which actually cloned the Canadian model. Interest in the task force methods has been and continues to be expressed by health departments and/or national health organizations in many other countries around the world.
Since its famous 1979 report, the Canadian task force on the periodic health examination has published several updates. These are presented in the Canadian Medical Association Journal for anglophone physicians and in I'Union medicale du Canada for the francophone medical practitioners. The Department of National Health and Welfare purchases reprints and distributes them to interested persons and institutions. In all, the task force methodology has been applied to some 200 different assessments both here and outside our borders.
In addition to supporting the development of world class standards in prevention, the federal government has been proactive in taking steps toward the implementation of prevention services. In 1987 the U.S. and

Canadian health departments, along with some private sector support, funded an international symposium implementing preventive services. It was held at l'Esterel, Quebec. Not only was this a colloquium of exemplary display by national co-operation, it really showed how, as I say, national co-operation was so important. It attracted many experts in prevention, experts from the United Kingdom, Europe and Australia.
The symposium at 1'Esterel made several recommendations about implementing prevented services. These included dissemination of recommendations of the Canadian task force on the periodic health examination; continuation of the task force's work; developing an implementation and infrastructure; educating health care professionals in a way that places more emphasis on prevention and working as part of a team; legislation such as immunization laws, helmet and seatbelt laws, and the non-smoking ordinances, an area in which our current federal government has provided superb leadership.

Mr. Speaker, on September 30 a major rally occurred in Rosetown, Saskatchewan, when over 4,000 farmers rallied to protest the lack
of action by the Government of Canada because of the tremendous financial crisis which is gripping many parts of Canada, including farm areas in Ontario and on the prairies. That was one of many rallies which occurred this fall.
On that day in the House of Commons, I asked the Deputy Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, the former Minister of Agriculture, the following question:
This afternoon in Rosetown, Saskatchewan, thousands of farmers are gathering to protest the lack of action by the government because they face the worst financial crisis in a generation for Canadian farmers.
Last winter, the government committed itself to providing a third line of defence financial assistance to these producers. When is the government going to provide this assistance?
The Minister of Finance and the Deputy Prime Minister responded, saying that in fact the Minister of Agriculture was going to attend that Rosetown rally and he would be putting forward a litany of programs and support the government has provided to the agricultural industry. In fact, what happened is the Minister of Agriculture attended the meeting, he sort of slid in the side door and out the back door. Practically nobody in the audience saw him and nobody heard him speak because he did not utter a word at the meeting. He came forth from the meeting and gave an interview to the media saying that he had no intention of providing further financial assistance to Canada's hard-pressed farmers.
Last week, several weeks after that event, more rallies occurred. There was a major one in Weybum a few weeks after this one with some 3,000 farmers. A little later over 7,000 farmers rallied in Regina. Finally the government announced belatedly that it was going to provide some $700 million worth of assistance to Canadian grain and oilseed producers. It did not say when or how it would pay for that. After several more weeks the government announced that it would pay about half of it some time around the first of next year and the rest of it some time in the new fiscal year after April 1.
The government's response to the financial crisis is simply not adequate. The financial crisis is caused by two factors. One is that the government sharply reduced its support programs last year by some $1.3 billion. That combined with the reduction in world prices for grains

and oilseeds has caused a major crisis for Canadian fanners. A year later the government is still nickeling and diming farmers: "Are we going to provide support January 1 and the other half in April?"
As a result we had another delegation last week in Ottawa. The new premier of Saskatchewan, ministers of agriculture from Alberta and Manitoba, leaders of the opposition, Lynda Haverstock from Saskatchewan, former leader from Alberta Nick Taylor and the leader from Manitoba Sharon Carstairs were all here to make further representations. It is time the government stopped fooling around and made these payments.

Mr. Speaker, some two months ago I asked a question in this House of the Minister of Finance concerning the very dangerous situation economically and socially facing the people of the Soviet Union as they approached the coming winter.
I pointed out that Alexander Yakovlev, former Soviet ambassador to Canada, a very respected citizen and one of the advisers to the new government, had said that empty pans are more dangerous than tanks. I urged the Minister of Finance to recognize that Canada should be showing leadership within the G-7 by supporting the urgent request of leaders of the Soviet Union and the various republics for aid as they approach the winter.
Here we are two months later and the situation is in fact desperate. We know, for example, that when the official in the Russian Federation, Mr. Yuri Luzhkov who is responsible for foreign economic affairs, met with the Minister for International Trade he mentioned the need for grain, fodder, meat, dairy products, sugar,
Adjournment Debate
vegetable oil, tea, cocoa and packing materials. He said that there is a desperate need now for food.
We know as well of the shortage of power, energy, and the fact that the minister of energy, Mr. Evgeny Pe-trayev, said: "We have never been so unprepared for winter". At least 40 cities would suffer serious shortages of power and heat during the winter. We know the shortages of basic medicines and disposable syringes and the looming disaster of AIDS which faces the people of the Soviet Union, of the independent nations, the Baltic nations and the independent nation of Ukraine. I might take this opportunity a couple of days after the people of Ukraine spoke out overwhelmingly in a free and democratic referendum-over 90 per cent spoke out in favour of independence, in favour of freedom, in favour of a free nation of Ukraine-to congratulate the people of Ukraine on that very historic decision.
I know that many of my constituents are of Ukrainian origin. Over a million Canadians celebrated this historic decision. I know as well that on this 100th anniversary of Ukrainian immigration to Canada we want to pay tribute to the tremendous role that Ukrainian Canadians have played in our society.
But much works remains to be done. The disaster of Chernobyl continues to cast a dark cloud over the children of Ukraine and of Byelorussia in particular. In my question I asked for our government to respond to the plea at the United Nations General Assembly for some $646 million in emergency aid to eliminate radioactivity from the food chain and to resettle the homeless victims of the Chernobyl disaster. Well, there still has been no response to that plea.
In the short time that remains I want again to say that the most effective response that we as Canadians can make to celebrate the independence of Ukraine, to celebrate the independence of the Baltic nations and to respond to the desperate plea of the other Soviet republics including particularly Russia, is to recognize that there must be direct aid now for food, medicine, energy, and of course to assist in averting environmental disaster. That is a plea we cannot ignore.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise tonight to discuss in the short time allotted to me a question which I asked the Deputy Prime Minister on October 3, 1991. It concerned Canada's announcement of its intention to terminate the memorandum of understanding on softwood lumber exports to the United States effective October 4, 1991.1 asked what contingency plan the government had to counter the inevitable American retaliatory action.
We all know that the memorandum of understanding on softwood lumber was never meant to be a permanent measure, yet it appears that the Americans do not know.
During the free trade debate this government told Canadians time and time again that we would get secure access to U.S. markets, and this is just one further example of how false this promise has been.
Now that the softwood lumber exports from Canada are under siege again, I can only assume that the Canadian government did not do its homework. Canada should win this decade-long dispute easily. Yet before the U.S. International Trade Commission in late November, Canada managed to take a good case and render it merely mediocre.
It has been reported that our representatives rambled on during the first round of the ITC meetings, getting everyone confused by giving a detailed description of the various species of wood and their uses. It fell on deaf ears.
Canada's case is simple and conclusive. Canada's lumber industry's share of the United States market has declined considerably from 33 per cent in 1985-86 to less than 26 per cent this year, reaching its lowest level in 13 years.
Between 1987, the year the memorandum of understanding came into effect, and 1991 the Canadian dollar has appreciated by 21 per cent, escalating from 72 cents in 1986 to roughly 88 cents today. The cumulative effect of our over-valued dollar and the 15 per cent export surtax have resulted in a total surcharge of about 36 per cent, thus driving down lumber profits and making Canadian lumber much less competitive in the U.S. markets.
The American interim bond posting measure will have the same impact as a self-imposed 15 per cent export surtax, not to say a self-inflicted wound which has yet to heal.
It is the recession, not the price of Canadian timber that is responsible for job losses in the U.S. lumber industry. B.C., Quebec, Ontario and other Canadian lumber producing provinces are not making any money in today's market, even with the allegation that our industry is being subsidized. Some 29,000 Canadian lumber industry workers have been laid off across the country since the inception of this MOU.
Since I was elected I have continuously pressured the government to seek a ruling from GATT. It has waited until November of this year to do so. Why a delay of three years? In the meantime the industry has lost its markets and it will be difficult to recoup them.
December 3, 1991

Therefore to conclude, I call upon this government to polish its presentation to the ITC and to insist that the Americans respect the spirit of the free trade agreement. The viability of this most important industry is at stake.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Plourde (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of International TVade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am answering this question concerning the measures taken by the government following the United States' decision to launch an investigation on the imposition of countervailing duties on softwood lumber and to require an interim bond for softwood lumber imported from Canada. From the beginning, we urged the United States Department of Commerce to exclude the Atlantic provinces from the investigation on countervailing duties. I am glad that it agreed.
We asked it to exclude Manitoba, Saskatchewan, the Nortwest Territories and the Yukon as well. Finally, the Commerce Department has restricted its investigation to the procedures for setting provincial stumpage rights, while in 1986, it examined 60 federal, federal-provincial and provincial programs and practices related to lumber.
In this case, our government's priority is to develop the best possible defence, in close co-operation with the provinces and the industry, to prove that U.S. allegations about subsidies are unfounded.
We have retained the services of a lawyer in Washington. The main provinces involved and the industry have retained an American lawyer to defend their interests.
Counsel for the government has maintained constant liaison with counsel for the provinces and the industry, ever since the United States started its investigation with a view to applying countervailing duties. So far, co-operation has been excellent.
We shall of course exercise all the rights we have under the free trade agreement. If necessary, we will appeal all unfavourable decisions to the binational dispute settlement mechanism provided under the agreement, an option that was not available in 1986.
Our government has also asked GATT to protect the interests of Canada. We have asked for the appointment of a special task force to determine whether stumpage rights imposed by a government constitute a subsidy that could be subject to countervail and whether the interim
Adjournment Debate
bond posting demanded by the United States conforms to the obligations the U.S. has under GATT.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, we are determined to defend our case to the very end, and we are confident that normal conditions for the lumber trade between Canada and the United States will be restored.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do apologize for the slight mix-up that we have had. I understood that this question was going to be about number four or five. I do apologize for not being here.
The government recognizes that the commodity prices are at a near record low and that many farmers are experiencing real difficulties. I want to say that our Prime Minister, our Minister of Agriculture, our Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds and our Minister of State for Agriculture are all very concerned, as are this caucus and this party very concerned about the state of agriculture. I think it would be fair to say that all members of this House of Commons equally share the concern that we and our producers are facing across this country.
The government certainly knows the importance of agriculture to our economy. That is why we have listened to farmers' concerns and why we have acted.
On November 21 this government announced details of the distribution of $800 million in special assistance to Canadian farmers. This money is in addition to the $640 million announced in April through the farm support and adjustment measures. The second round of the
